By leveraging the principles of molecular robotics, we have adapted and refined existing methods to assess radio signal strength while accounting for a drone's limited flight capabilities. To achieve this, we have developed an adaptive, decision-theoretic framework that allows a single drone to explore an unknown environment while continuously collecting signal strength readings. Our approach is benchmarked against various comparison methods, and extensive simulations, as well as real-world experiments using a quadcopter, have shown that it is comparable to or superior to fixed-path exploration methods in terms of coverage and efficiency.

This research presents an innovative approach where Hidden Markov Models are used to identify anomalies in time series data by analyzing their probability profiles. An anomaly detection method has been developed that compares normal and abnormal cases, using a probability evaluation technique known as the Gauge. This method Assembles, Traverses, and Evaluates (ATE) the Hidden Markov Model to obtain the probability timeline, and then extracts features from this timeline to distinguish between anomaly types. To classify anomalies, this method leverages the unique characteristics of each, where normal cases have a distinct, plateaued probability pattern and abnormal cases exhibit a significant decrease in probability within a short time frame. What differentiates one type of anomaly from another is the relative probability values at the anomaly peak. This anomaly identification method can automatically determine the start and end times of an anomaly without manual input and produces classification results based on the calculated features. Experimental findings on real-world data showcase the method's anomaly detection capabilities and its reliance on the specific characteristics of each data set to classify anomalies effectively.

This study investigates the effectiveness of a unified authentication system using audio, visual, and thermal data. We gathered a diverse dataset from 220 subjects, collecting face, ear, and finger thermal images, as well as voice samples via microphone. To create a robust authentication system, we examined various feature combinations from different modalities. Notably, our results show that using thermal data alone surpasses the performance of using sole audio or video information. We also explored the impact of varying environmental conditions on feature robustness and discovered that using thermal data is more resilient than audio or video alone in difficult scenarios.

The quality of pre-training data significantly impacts the performance of subsequent downstream tasks. However, preparing such a large dataset with high accuracy is impractically challenging. To overcome this issue, we propose leveraging existing knowledge from diverse external sources, including text sources not used in the model's pre-training. We develop a novel, low-effort approach to effectively incorporate this information into the model. The method involves adapting a span-level attention mechanism during the decoding process, allowing the model to gain insights from relevant external texts. Our experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that this method enhances the model's performance by approximately 2% in terms of accuracy, without necessitating substantial manual intervention or additional training. Moreover, we find that this approach is particularly effective in tasks facing data shortages, achieving improved results comparable to those of those tasks with ample data.

When dealing with a single observation from a mixture of two distributions, the likelihood function doesn't have a minimum within its interior. To analyze a single observation, we consider contributions from both the mixture and the combination of its components, resulting in a modified likelihood function. This approach leads to a consistent estimator of the mixture parameter, which behaves well in terms of bias. Additionally, this method produces reliable confidence intervals for the mixture parameter. Simulation results illustrate the performance of these intervals under various scenarios. The methodology is successfully applied to two real-world problems, sampling a spherical solid and analyzing a type of rock structure.

Achieving differential privacy on aggregated data with Safeguarded Aggregation has a confidentiality issue when the values of consecutive data entries are highly dependent. This occurs because the disclosure of a single data value may reveal information about an adjacent value, potentially compromising privacy. To address this problem, we developed an improved model of differential privacy, one-sided differential privacy based on dependent data, and designed a secure aggregation protocol that aligns with this new model and provides efficient communication.

Astronomers have identified a significant CO gap within the disk surrounding the young star AS 209 via a thorough examination of the data collected through the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-creating Scales (MAPS) project at sub-millimeter wavelengths. This CO gap is situated near the dust gap previously detected using SPICA/POLHEMs and ALMA data at comparable wavelengths. We have analyzed the spectral line data collected through ALMA's observation of the AS 209 system and discovered that the CO emission originates from a layer approximately 10 astronomical units above the midplane of the disk. This CO emission can be categorized into three distinct components: a narrow peak at 42.18 MHz and two broader emission patterns. By calculating the kinetic temperature within this region, we have found it to be approximately 30 K, which is consistent with the temperature detected through continuum analysis. We have also found that the CO emission is significantly concentrated within the CO gap, which suggests that the CO molecules are present in lower concentrations compared to other areas of the disk. This observation can be attributed to either the CO molecules being removed due to chemical processing or the CO molecules being moved away due to gas dynamics. To better understand this phenomenon, we have created a model that incorporates both chemical and physical processes. This model reveals that the CO gap can be explained by either case, which highlights the need for further observation and simulation.

Researchers across various scientific fields consistently gather large datasets, known as time-tagged measurements, which are typically analyzed using specialized software or even custom-developed tools.  However, these datasets often remain underutilized due to a lack of appropriate software support, forcing scientists to resort to creating their own tools or using general-purpose platforms, which inevitably fail to cater to their unique requirements.  To address this issue, we have devised a versatile and feature-rich platform, referred to as TTMe, designed specifically for examining time-tagged measurements.  Developed as an open-source Python library, TTMe offers an intuitive graphical user interface and a range of advanced features, including data import, visualization, analysis, and storage capabilities, as well as customizable data labeling and sorting options, all of which are easily accessible through a simple and intuitive menu system.  Furthermore, TTMe allows users to create and execute complex data processing workflows using a drag-and-drop interface, thereby eliminating the need for intricate coding.  With its vast potential applications across many scientific domains, TTMe is particularly suitable for examining time-resolved data in fields like astronomy, biology, medicine, and networking.  As a community-driven initiative, TTMe is now available for download on GitHub, along with comprehensive documentation and related resources, and we invite users to contribute to its further development as a collaborative project.

We establish the existence of mild solutions for a mean field game involving a large number of controls with movements constrained within a limited area. To achieve this, we first separate the problem into two components: a transport equation and a optimization issue with constraints. We successfully find a solution for the transport equation, which satisfies the required regularity. Furthermore, by using the regularity of the transport equation, we prove the existence of a mild solution for the optimization problem. Our approach is particularly significant because it enables the use of large data, which simplifies the application to mean field games.

Stellar threads are considered an essential aspect of galaxy evolution research, despite not fitting traditional classification categories. This study re-evaluates their significance by comparing the spatial distribution of stellar threads in the Milky Way, through the use of a machine learning algorithm and a dot representation of the galaxy's structure. The results show that these stellar threads do not possess unique information for mapping the galaxy's center or orientation. Therefore, they can be replaced by other, more straightforward features, without compromising the accuracy of the mapping process. Consequently, the usefulness of stellar threads in the context of the Milky Way is called into question.

The main goal of visual discrepancy detection is to identify obvious fashion mismatches in terms of item type, category, style, and price, using a single image of an outfit. This process is crucial for both online shopping platforms seeking to remove non-fitting items from user searches and fashion retailers aiming to enhance user experiences. Since visual discrepancy detection is a relatively new area of research, there is currently limited information available. To tackle this challenge, we introduce the Visual Discrepancy Detection (VDD) task and propose a suitable dataset, called Fashion-Weakly, which consists of annotated images along with corresponding text descriptions. However, existing dataset collections, like Fashion-Weakly, do not have sufficient data for effective training. To overcome this limitation, we develop a dataset augmentation technique by leveraging a massive fashion image corpus and conduct a contrastive pre-training approach using a transformer-based model. This pre-trained model is then fine-tuned to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the Fashion-Weakly dataset. Moreover, we release the first open-source benchmark, called the Fashion-Weakly dataset, along with our proposed approach, called VICTOR, which outperforms baseline models.

In recent years, quantum information science has experienced significant advancements, particularly in understanding and exploiting quantum effects for enhanced information processing tasks. However, the rate of breakthroughs has slowed since the early 2000s, and there is now a need for overarching theoretical frameworks that can unify and guide further research. One such general approach is the use of resource theories. This report serves as an introduction to the resource theoretical description of generalized nonclassical light and highlights key innovations and applications within the field.

As the need for training neural networks on large datasets grows, the challenges posed by diverse system environments and slow communication links become more significant. Federated learning offers a promising framework for developing decentralized models, capable of being trained on distributed data without relocating it. However, the asynchronous nature of FL encounters difficulties in handling differences in computation time at clients. To address this, researchers proposed a solution involving buffered aggregation, which synchronizes client updates based on a shared reference point. Despite mitigating the issue, this approach introduces new challenges, including the requirement for synchronized gradient magnitudes and slow convergence rates. To overcome these limitations, this paper presents an alternative solution called Unconstrained Gradient Accumulation (UGA), an optimized buffered asynchronous aggregation technique for distributed neural network training. By UGA's buffer exchange is not dependent on stopping criteria such as gradient norm, it can exchange updates more frequently, even if local training times vary greatly. Moreover, UGA's innovative buffer exchange algorithm ensures that the final model is calibrated consistently. Experimental results demonstrate that UGA outperforms traditional federated learning methods on both a image classification and a text-based task, despite only differing in their aggregation procedure.

This paper extends the operational calculus to the space of polynomial tempered distributions, exploring a novel approach through first-order differential operators and their inverses. We define a shift operator and establish key approximation formulas within the context of polynomial tempered distributions. Furthermore, we develop inverse mappings for differential operators, including the application of fractional linear transformations. This framework is grounded in a modified algebra of polynomial tempered distributions, analogous to the original Weyl algebra.

We expand upon the concept of the Shadow Dimension, initially introduced by Linné Baker and Paddy Gallagher in 2020, linking it to the Swampland framework. A key aspect of the theory is that the Shadow Dimension's presence correlates with the occurrence of gravitational anomalies. Additionally, we investigate scenarios where the Shadow Dimension's value is determined by the density of hidden dark matter comprised of primordial black holes.

Floating debris rafts are ubiquitous across various scales, ranging from tsunami victim survival to ice melting. Despite their widespread occurrence, there has been limited research on the mechanics of floating rafts. To address this gap, we have conducted a series of experiments and analyses examining the behavior of a raft as it approaches collapse under two different types of loading. Our findings reveal that when a raft is subjected to a uniformly distributed load, it undergoes a systematic and predictable failure. However, when subjected to a discretely applied load, the outcome is more complex, and the physics are reminiscent of crack formation in materials. Just like fractures in metals, these 'fractures' pose challenges for the further analysis and understanding of the system. To overcome this obstacle, we have introduced a new concept, the Fracture Density, which enables us to simplify the discretized load into a more coherent and understandable form. Our research also includes an in-depth comparison with the theoretical model of an elastic plate, as well as an analysis of the implications of our discoveries.

This study presents an innovative approach to significantly enhance hole mobility in p-GaN by aligning the lattice in the direction perpendicular to the substrate. Our results demonstrate that this anisotropic strain, achieved through the incorporation of ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ via molecular beam epitaxy, yields a notable improvement in hole mobility. Specifically, with the optimal strain conditions, the hole mobility in p-GaN exceeds that of unstrained material, with the maximum achieved to date at 13.9 cm$^2$/Vs. Furthermore, our research reveals that this anisotropic strain modulates the conical band structure of p-GaN, facilitating easier hole movement and thereby boosting mobility. Ultimately, this novel technique offers a promising solution for optimizing p-GaN-based optical and electrical devices.

Marine robots are becoming increasingly essential for ocean research, allowing for efficient gathering of underwater data. Their applications extend to coral reef monitoring, sea floor detection, and water quality analysis. To navigate effectively in the complex ocean environment, marine robots utilize various path planning techniques. Unlike robots operating in structured settings, ocean robots must consider dynamic changes in their environment, including ocean currents, which impact their movement. To account for these dynamics, existing navigation methods often rely on manually created maps or real-time data streams. This paper presents a novel approach, Sparse GP, that leverages historical robot data to learn the ocean currents' patterns without the need for external input. The proposed method uses Gaussian Process regression to analyze the robot's past movements, identifying the probability distribution of the current vector for any given location. The results show that Sparse GP outperforms compared to baseline methods using self-supervised learning on simulated and actual ocean current data.

This paper explores unique rim-unique transcendental entire solutions derived from Darboux and Calapso transformations of isothermal surfaces with a single boundary. Additionally, the study generalizes these transformations to the entire complex plane and provides biholomorphic mapping evidence for certain meromorphic entire real-analytic functions.

This course note examines an established method for nonparametrically estimating multivariate conditional expectation functions, along with its associated limiting distribution and efficient estimation methods.
This paper expresses various identities involving $\lambda$-versions of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind using a cumulative generating function.

Research on linking existing knowledge graphs with future developments is gaining traction in the field of knowledge graph completion. Despite the potential of this area, a notable aspect is the lack of substantial research in this field. To address this gap, our work focuses on link forecasting in temporal knowledge graphs with a two-stage approach that utilizes a static framework. By doing so, we are able to enhance the existing literature on this topic and provide insights through experimental results.

Two row-finite graph algebras are robustly equivalent if their universal graphs are equivalent, whereas two row-finite graphs themselves are robustly equivalent if they have equivalent universal graphs, regardless of scaling. This notion extends to C*-algebras, where two row-finite graphs' C*-algebras are robustly equivalent if their respective universal graphs are equivalent. In the context of graph algebras, this notion does not conflict with traditional shift equivalence, but it is known to be non-degenerate in the context of C*-algebras generally.

Using the T-Matrix approach and an advanced propagator framework at finite magnetic field and parton momentum, we study heavy quark fragmentation and distribute heavy hadrons, such as D, Ds, B and Bs mesons, and B and Bs hadrons, preserving $SU(2)_V \times SU(2)_A$ symmetry. By doing so, we identify anisotropic fragmentation functions and pattern, spatially and numerically, and investigate the effect of magnetic field on heavy quark fragmentation for both low and high Landau levels.

To improve question answering, we're enhancing large language models with knowledge graph reasoning capabilities. Our proposed method involves adapting these models to infer relevant knowledge graph entities, leveraging simplified natural language that our model can effectively process. We're introducing a new dataset, GQA-Entity, to facilitate this, as well as evaluating our method on existing question answering datasets. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with significant performance improvements on various datasets.

We present a straightforward method of creating high-dimensional bipartite expander graphs by taking coverings of certain high-dimensional bipartite graphs, such as the random left regular bipartite graph, and demonstrating that the resulting graphs remain expanders in a high-dimensional sense. To achieve this, we establish a spectral decomposition of these graphs and show that all non-trivial spectral components have spectral norms less under a certain threshold, thereby guaranteeing a high-dimensional expander structure. This innovative approach enables the construction of high-dimensional bipartite expander graphs with significantly larger girth, at least girth 4, in comparison to previous methods. Furthermore, by incorporating edge-weighted random fields, we construct high-dimensional small-girth bipartite expander graphs, offering a potential solution for the Coppersmith-Shamir problem.

Recent developments in natural language models have shown that these models can be easily misled when confronted with crafted language prompts, which have significant implications for their practical applications. The effectiveness of language prompts is often evaluated in tasks that require them to anticipate a user's response or to facilitate effective communication. However, there is limited research on how these prompts function in scenarios where the task involves making a choice. To address this, we conducted an extensive zero-shot evaluation of language prompts across six diverse choice tasks, which revealed that prompts are highly effective in providing guidance, but are also adaptable and resilient. Moreover, our study identified distinct characteristics of prompts that excel in various tasks, as well as explored the potential of these prompts in other areas, such as their ability to anticipate malicious uses or to convey a particular tone.

We explore the concept of $\mathscr{L}$-invariants in its most fundamental form, 
articulating its purpose and then examining its connection to a simpler model 
for better understanding, specifically within the context of motivations for 
$p$-adic Langlands.

A cutting-edge method for detecting microwave fields using Rydberg atoms has been developed, which could serve as a precise indicator of magnetic field strength in atomic, molecular, and optical physics research as well as in quantum information sciences. This technique, which uses multi-frequency microwaves, can provide detailed insights into microwave conditions through its atomic responses at various Rydberg levels. However, the complexity of Rydberg states and interactions with other atoms or photons limit their practical use, driving the development of a deep learning approach to improve detection accuracy. By integrating deep learning and Rydberg atom research, we have successfully created a deep neural network that can accurately sense both strong and weak microwave fields even in the presence of atoms. This breakthrough has the potential to increase the accuracy of Rydberg state research and quantum computations.

The young, compact dwarf galaxy UGC 8839 boasts one of the lowest rates of star formation activity in similar nearby galaxies. This unusual suppression of star formation has led researchers to assume that the galaxy must have an exceptionally large reservoir of cold molecular gas, which would otherwise be visible as a broad disk in the far-infrared radiation. To resolve this enigma, researchers have employed the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array to map the molecular gas distribution in UGC 8839 at high spatial resolution, and their findings include a distinctive, hyper-compressed disk of gas surrounding the galaxy's center. This over-pression may be attributed to a hidden, radio-emitting outburst in the galaxy, and it is proposed that the distinctive gas pattern is a result of the galaxy's central star-forming episode, which has created and sustained this characteristic structure.

For a quasiregular self-mapping in 3D space, we establish the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set and distinguishing set respectively. Both sets' dimensions are found to be either 2 or 3, with the difference stemming solely from the absence or presence of fixed points. Notably, these results contradict the behavior of the Julia set in the quadratic family, where the presence of a fixed point influences dimension beyond a pure 2 value.

Previous studies have identified a diurnal gravity wave (GW) cycle in the Mars atmosphere, specifically observed in the upper atmosphere by various spacecraft, between 140-220 km above mean sea level. This cycle is most pronounced in the neutral atmosphere, particularly in the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Mars Climate Information Center dataset, which combines data from multiple spacecraft. Analysis of the dataset reveals that GW amplitudes follow a predictable pattern at each spacecraft's altitude, with a daily cycle that peaks around sunset and nonsolar periods. This study investigates the cause of these daily cycles in the upper atmosphere, specifically in the ionosphere and the Mars Science Laboratory's atmospheric electron density measurements, and finds that they are consistent across various Mars orbiters' data. Furthermore, Mars Atmospheric and Environmental Monitoring by the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter shows that daily cycles in the upper atmosphere are not present in atmospheric electron density at an altitude of around 220 km, suggesting that these daily cycles are transmitted from the ionosphere to the upper atmosphere, but with reduced amplitude. Analysis of the atmospheric and ionospheric data during GW events shows that these daily cycles are not random but follow a predictable pattern. This suggests that atmospheric tides play a role in the daily cycles in the upper atmosphere, which is consistent with previous studies.

The ALICE experiment has been at the forefront of studying particle production in proton-lead and lead-proton collisions at the LHC, providing valuable insights into the gluon distribution in these systems. Our findings reveal that the proton and lead nuclei interact through photon-mediated processes in ultra-peripheral collisions, resulting in the creation of charmonium particles such as the J/ψ. Our analysis of these interactions has yielded a J/ψ cross-section measure that matches theoretical predictions based on the proton structure function, while also offering a way to explore the nature of these interactions further. This presentation will discuss our recent findings on J/ψ production in Pb-Pb ultra-peripheral collisions, focusing on how the cross section changes with energy and rapidity. Our measurements show that J/ψ production decreases with increasing centrality, which may be attributed to the effects of shadowing or other phenomena. Additionally, we will discuss how our findings agree with theoretical predictions based on different models of nuclear structure, providing a unique perspective on the subject.

Sound waves visible to the naked eye create both audible and inaudible ripples
in the air. Researchers reevaluate the underlying physics of a phenomenon
known as "visible sound," acknowledging that traditional notions of frequency
and wavelength may be insufficient. A novel framework for sound generation is
introduced, allowing for digital precision and a more intuitive creative process
via visual editing software. By applying digital forces, artists can configure the
shape and properties of sound waves, resulting in novel patterns of sound. Early
adoption examples demonstrate the potential of this new method, and it is
expected to expand the sound design palette in various fields including music,
film, architecture, and performance art.

Sequential temporal data typically requires significant sequential information to be analyzed, making it distinct from general data. To tackle this, a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) can be leveraged, although the inherent vanishing gradient problem it poses typically hinders optimal performance. In order to develop an effective RNN for handling large sequential data, we explored various techniques for enhancing RNN architectures, including the incorporation of a memory mechanism. Our empirical analysis entailed comparing the performance of various RNN designs based on their training strategies and the use of a dedicated memory component. Interestingly, our results pointed to the superiority of an RNN with a memory component when trained using smaller mini-batch sizes.

To find a balance between pandemic control and economic relief, we've developed a model that allows for simultaneous optimization. By incorporating both health and economic costs, along with the timing of interventions, our model provides a precise solution. We demonstrate that the optimal policy is universal, depending only on the rate at which new infections multiply and the rate at which deaths accumulate. Furthermore, our approach reveals a critical but often overlooked factor: the speed of demographic changes within a population. Without consideration of demographic shifts, our model's outcome becomes even more straightforward, allowing for the maximum extension of the time available for policy adjustments.

In various real-world applications, vast datasets are continually collected at incredible speeds, with the goal of updating ever-evolving machine learning models. However, as data volumes grow, selecting the most beneficial information for analysis becomes increasingly complex, especially when faced with a plethora of incoming data streams. To address this challenge, our research focuses on optimizing data utilization within machine learning pipelines by identifying and prioritizing the most crucial samples, thereby maximizing the models' accuracy and efficiency. By extending the concept of Shapley Value analysis to multi-stage machine learning workflows, our framework provides actionable insights that guide decision-making and guide both data curation and model development strategies. Through hands-on experiments, we have thoroughly validated the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

This survey article presents an introduction to various statistical models, combinatorial methods and topological techniques that serve as essential tools in modern enumerative geometry. It specifically outlines the key concepts used to study the numerical values and algebraic structures associated with counting problems in algebraic geometry, with a focus on proving rigorous statements about these numerical values.

Under normal conditions, the triangular lattice of Mn$_3$Sn exhibits anomalous Hall effects despite being an antiferromagnet, not a ferromagnet. At high pressures (over 10 kbar), Mn$_3$Sn transitions into a zigzag spin state with a byproduct of weakening its anomalous Hall effect. Crystallographic analysis during pressure treatment (up to 20 kbar) in a single crystal of Mn$_3$Sn revealed that the spin state transformed into a long-awaited long-period spin state. As a result, the anomalous Hall effect significantly decreased by an order of magnitude. High-pressure X-ray diffraction and resistivity measurements confirm that the pressure-stable spin state is a long-period arrangement.

Relation extraction is a crucial task in Natural Language Processing that enables the identification, parsing, and categorization of relationships between entities in a sentence. Despite significant advancements in NLP, this area remains underdeveloped for full-scale application in comparison to classification and sentiment analysis. A relatively recent approach using deep neural networks has improved the accuracy of relation extraction, outperforming earlier rule-based and machine learning techniques. To understand the effectiveness and simplicity of deep neural network-based models, we conducted a comprehensive survey of 90 datasets and 248 models, revealing that a fully supervised approach using simple recurrent neural network architectures often yields the best results. Our analysis and empirical observations are presented to highlight the state-of-the-art in relation extraction using deep neural networks.

This article examines a boundary value problem that combines Steklov and Robin conditions on a domain with a single boundary. We start by proving an exact formula for the spectral weight of each eigenvalue in the Steklov problem and demonstrate that this eigenvalue possesses compact geometric significance. Next, we establish a characterization of the Dirichlet eigenvalue, a characterization that resembles the original Riesz compactness principle. Finally, using a relatively standard method, we prove the validity of the classical Dirichlet-Bruhat problem in L^p norm for the Laplace operator on a domain with bounded smooth boundary.

In many fields, researchers often create composite graphs to illustrate complex relationships between different entities and the relationships among those entities. However, traditional methods may not adequately capture the interconnected nature of these relationships, leading to incomplete representations. Hypergraphs, a type of higher-order graph, offer a more accurate way to encode these relationships and can be used to improve existing composite graph representations. To take advantage of this, we need effective methods to transplant features from lower-order graphs to hypergraphs and vice versa, a task that has received limited attention in previous research. We fill this gap by developing the guided hypergraph reconstruction algorithm, which utilizes a part of the graph to transfer attributes to a higher-order structure, and employs a projection-based approach to achieve this. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and our results show that it outperforms existing hypergraph reconstruction methods.

To develop effective computer-aided diagnosis systems for chest X-rays, it is crucial to create high-quality, diverse datasets with detailed annotations. However, creating such datasets poses challenges, primarily the variability in annotation types required for different applications. In this research, we establish a comprehensive dataset of chest X-ray images, along with detailed annotations for various conditions, drawing inspiration from the MS-COD dataset's rich annotation set for medical image analysis. Our dataset is created using a combination of expert radiologists' feedback and an automatic annotation tool trained on CT projections of chest X-rays. The results show that our approach yields accurate annotations for both finding identification and semantic segmentation. Moreover, experiments using a cross-validation strategy on internal validation data reveal strong correlations between annotation difficulty levels and diagnostic challenges for human radiologists.

Ozaydin initially noted down the relationship $4-\chi(M)$ $\leq$ $|\xi_+| \leq$ 2+ $\chi(M)$ for any orientable three-dimensional manifold M with $\chi(M)$ denoting the Euler characteristic of M and $\xi_+$ representing the Thurston norm of M. Our findings reveal that the lower bound can be eliminated, specifically we found an example where $|\xi_+|=$ 2 and $|\xi_+|<$ $\chi(M)$.

We developed an entropy-based criterion to identify and analyze anisotropic emission patterns in microcavity lasers. By using the maximum incoherence approximation, our approach entropically measures the polarization-dependent radiation from microcavity lasers, thereby distinguishing isotropic, unidirectional, and bidirectional emission phenomena. Through calculations and comparative analysis with both classical and quantum theory, we demonstrated the capability of our entropy criterion to identify all three types of directional emissions. This findings provide a foundation for exploring the relationship between directional emission and entropy, thereby contributing to the understanding of spontaneous radiation.

Our research examines the cost stability of cryptocurrencies as a means of exchange 
within a dynamic framework derived from Walras' general equilibrium theory. 
By dynamic framework, we mean one that incorporates time and a flow of services 
in the model, as opposed to the traditional static model which only considers a 
point in time and a stock of goods. The model assumes a two-cryptocurrency, 
two-goods economy with the cryptocurrencies serving as a means of payment, and 
the goods representing consumption and production activities. The model's 
stability condition is based on a specific criterion which must be met in order to 
prevent excessive fluctuations in the exchange rates of the two cryptocurrencies 
relative to the two goods. The model reveals that when the absolute value of a 
particular variable exceeds a certain threshold, it can cause extreme price 
fluctuations, potentially leading to a crisis in the payment system.

A key component in understanding the dynamics of a wide range of systems is having a theoretically sound formulation of their noise mechanisms. For certain non-equilibrium quantum systems, a specific type of correlated noise can be expected to influence their behavior. By assuming this noise to be weak, researchers can utilize the reverse scattering technique to derive precise analytical formulas that accurately capture the impact of the noise. This noise correction can be re-expressed in a form that closely resembles the usual Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation, except for a system that is now quantum-based. The resulting solution to this modified KPZ equation is seen to align with numerical simulations, but only up to a particular time scale. Beyond this point, the system's behavior becomes increasingly sensitive to the characteristics of the noise, making it essential to utilize the reverse scattering approach to fully comprehend these dynamics.

Our research focuses on extremely small-scale turbulence within the solar wind's compressive patterns, which are too tiny to be detected by magnetic field measurements. By analyzing data from spacecraft voltages, we identified and analyzed a significant number of these tiny compressive structures, observed multiple times from different spacecraft. From three Spacecraft, we found consistent patterns in the detected waves, with characteristics similar to those observed using electric field measurements. However, unlike electric field measurements, spacecraft voltages often miss some of these tiny waves, which are then detected at a different time. This difference in detection is mainly due to the movement of the spacecraft and the structure's extremely small size. As a result, we found that the majority of the detected tiny waves are aligned in a specific direction and are often found in pairs, with a consistent spacing between them. This spacing varies depending on several factors, including velocity and frequency.

To produce high-energy, attosecond pulses in the XUV and soft X-ray range, researchers utilize the incoherent overlap of many individual FEL pulses. A modified variant of the chirp-taper technique has been developed to achieve this, involving the optimization of gain to produce a highly incoherent pulse population within a single amplifier section. Subsequent optimization of feedback loop settings enables the extraction of attosecond pulses with up to 100 femtosecond macropulse durations at the FLASH facility. Operating the gain material at optimal temperature significantly reduces pulse broadening, while sophisticated algorithmic solutions enable the identification of an optimized feedback loop setting that produces the shortest possible pulses.

Estimating the behavior of complex layered viscous shear flows remains a significant challenge in understanding the formation of turbidites and other thick, coarse-grained sedimentary sequences. To address this issue, a new approach is developed using the principle of physical optics, which is grounded in a deterministic formulation based on the Helmholtz equation. This method is enhanced by incorporating a novel extension of the Faddeev green's function technique, facilitating the estimation of thick sequences from multiple thin beds. Through numerical modeling, the approach is demonstrated to provide an accurate and reliable method for analyzing multiple layered sequences, as well as individual beds, with and without the presence of turbulence.

To combat unfair electoral manipulation, also known as gerrymandering, researchers have created various metrics. However, many of these metrics have been contested as being flawed or biased. As such, this study presents a new, more robust metric that not only outperforms existing ones but also provides voters with direct insight into the fairness of their election results. This proposed metric is inspired by a novel idea where voters' political affiliations are represented as temperatures, with extreme temperatures heating up certain districts to influence the outcome. By analyzing the effects of temperature changes, our method effectively measures the unfair manipulation of election results.

Textile flaw identification is of significant importance for maintaining the quality of textiles. Since patterned textiles contain intricate designs, identifying flaws in these is even more challenging than in plain textiles. Existing methods are limited as they often require expert annotation or rely on training, which can be time-consuming. To overcome these challenges, this paper proposes an improved texture descriptor, GHOG, and combines it with low-rank decomposition to automatically detect flaws in patterned textiles without the need for additional information. The efficacy of this method was tested on various patterned textiles, and experimental results show its superiority over existing techniques.

A well-established approach to image-based navigation in robotics utilizes information-theoretic measures, such as relative entropy, to create a objective function for training visual navigation tasks. However, this method's performance is hindered by the local minimization of its objective function, leading to incomplete exploration of the image space and weak correlation between the agent's actions and the resulting images. In our study, we introduce a new approach that leverages reinforcement learning to extend the training process for image-based navigation tasks. By combining the original information-theoretic objective function with a reinforcement learning reward signal, our approach maximizes both image novelty and the navigational efficiency of the agent. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method in simulated 2D and 3D environments as well as real-world robotic experiments, demonstrating its superior performance compared to previous image-based navigation techniques.

In the framework of Bondi's radiative collapse model, the rate at which a black hole's mass decreases can be understood as a result of an incoming mass flow from infinity. This mass flow rate is influenced by two primary factors: the velocity of the incoming flux and its density. By assuming that this velocity cannot exceed the speed of light, a maximum mass flow rate is established, amounting to approximately 2.66 x 10^18 kilograms per second. This theoretical limit may have implications for models of black hole evaporation and cosmological phenomena.

Our theoretical model explores how the initial burst of star formation in the early universe influences the merging of black holes within the remaining stellar clusters. Specifically, we focus on the impact of primordial mass distribution on the merging of individual black hole pairs within these clusters. Our analysis also considers how the spatial arrangement of black holes within these clusters is affected by their mass. We find that a significant portion of the gravitational waves detected by LISA will originate from these cosmic stellar remnants, with a detectable merger rate that is about 10 to 100 times higher than previously estimated. Moreover, the gravitational waves emitted by these cosmic events will provide valuable insights into the early universe, including the nature of the first heavy elements and the conditions within the cosmic plasma immediately after the formation of the first stars and galaxies.

Incident convergence in power distribution networks has been a major issue, leading to widespread outages and heightened safety risks during extreme weather conditions. Pinning down incident locations is a particularly onerous challenge, as they often go undetected until severe anomalies appear in energy consumption or voltage levels. Our proposed approach tackles this problem by using smart meter data to identify incidents in sub-feeder sections, allowing for early detection and reduced consequences of incidents. First, we develop a data-driven method to pinpoint incident locations by analyzing changes in energy consumption patterns. Then, we utilize a statistical technique to filter out false positives and pinpoint specific incident locations. Finally, we verify our approach's effectiveness with simulations using a 12-node test network.

Our study of X(3872) decays focuses on two processes: X(3872) dissociating into a J/psi photon and a pi particle, and into a J/psi and a pi-pi pair. The first of these occurs through an intermediate state of just pi and includes a contribution from the orbital angular momentum of the system. The magnitude of this effect is calculated and found to be significant. The second process allows the X(3872) to be composed of different quark combinations, and its nature is influenced by these possible constituents and the parameters of the decay route. The probability distributions of the X(3872) composed of different quark combinations are found through Bayesian analysis in relation to the X(3872) decay pattern. The study also determines the X(3872) mass through a charge conservation principle in relation to its two-pion decay ratio and the ratio of radiative and two-pion decay rates.

We provide a comprehensive description of smooth quadrics in terms of a specific category of stable objects within a family of finite-dimensional algebra representations, and use this description to characterize smooth quadrics in terms of their properties in this categorical framework. 

Similar to the case of hyperbolic quadrics, our results in this chapter achieve this characterization through an analysis of a particular sequence of simple objects within this representation, and the resulting relationships between stable objects and their ranks. 

Additionally, the method employed to derive these results in this chapter differs from that used for hyperbolic quadrics, instead utilizing properties of an important class of objects known as line bundles, and instead using a different characterization of quadrics that involves these line bundles. 

Line bundles play a significant role in the study of algebraic surfaces, with their use dating back to major works by Iversen and Sato, among others.

We introduce TextWorldExpress, an ultra-high-performance text-based game engine designed for AI training, with the capability to process over one million actions per second. TextWorldExpress is significantly faster than the original TextWorld, with a speed increase of more than 500 times. TextWorldExpress enables the creation of large-scale text-based game environments with reduced computational complexity by leveraging multiple CPU cores and techniques such as asynchronized rendering and command processing. TextWorldExpress facilitates the rapid production of datasets with specified characteristics, including adversarial examples, for the training of intelligent language models. TextWorldExpress provides open access to its platform and related tools through dedicated repositories.

We develop a system of A-spatial operators for studying Topological Insulators in a rigorous, flaw-free context and then introduce various types of errors to relate our work to existing research. Special attention is given to using $C^*$-algebras and functors to characterize extended symmetry classes of Topological Insulators on general spaces, encompassing electron systems with interactions and multiproduct spaces with fluxes.

This research focuses on $p$-harmonic functions in two-dimensional sectors, specifically those defined by $|x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta| < 1$. We establish the limits within which these functions have meaningful growth rates in comparison to $|x+y|^{\frac{p-1}{p}}$, where $\theta$ is within the interval $(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2})$. We also investigate how these estimates are affected by the angle $\theta$ and demonstrate that for values close to $\frac{\pi}{2}$, the growth rate can be compared to $|x+y|^{\frac{p-1}{p}-\varepsilon}$ for any arbitrarily small $\varepsilon$.

Identifying the most severe weather and sea conditions is crucial for maritime risk management, yet existing multivariate models have significant drawbacks when applying spatial statistics, losing their utility in the process. To address this, we develop a new spatial model for extreme ocean conditions, focusing on Euclidean space, and one that can effectively capture correlations among multiple variables. Our new model, which is based on peak exceedance processes, can flexibly accommodate both temporal and spatial dependencies. By applying this model to extreme wave data from the North Atlantic, we demonstrate its strong potential for practical use in maritime risk assessment.

We establish a general theorem describing the finiteness of non-constant polynomial or rational functions over number fields, which can be applied to solve multiple distinct cases. The solutions to these cases were previously proposed by Boxer, over a $Q$-basis, and our approach enables a similar outcome with a number field of any degree. Additionally, our method allows for the consideration of cases involving functions that are not defined at every point and, consequently, leads to a more refined statement, distinct from Boxer's result.

Our approach, called MADS, is a general method for adapting robot tasks learned from human demonstrations in similar but altered environments. It combines a new point-to-point navigation method with our modified Iterative Closest Point algorithm to efficiently match the new environment with the cached map. MADS relies on connecting landmarks instead of solely relying on proximity, which enables seamless transition between maps on a curved geometric surface without getting stuck in local minima. Furthermore, MADS transports points along this surface using geodesic curves, which allows it to operate without a global map, making it more suitable for tasks like robotics and virtual reality. We've successfully tested MADS in various scenarios with significant domain differences and found that it outperforms the traditional ICp algorithm by accurately aligning maps in as little as half the time.

In a study of Higgs boson pair creation at the LHC's 13 TeV proton-proton collider, our analysis focuses on the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ decay pathway. To achieve this, we employ the matrix element technique in combination with a parton shower simulation. This approach is compared to a three-lepton analysis and our findings indicate that the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ decay pathway can be effectively utilized to detect Higgs boson pairs at the LHC.

We investigate how a robot can determine the three-dimensional structure of an object through observation alone by watching it spin around its axis. When an object rotates, its surface features, like markings or patterns, produce consistent visual cues that indicate its true 3D shape. We develop a robot vision algorithm that extracts and analyzes these cues, using a simplified model that requires minimal prior knowledge. The algorithm is then tested in a simulated environment to verify its effectiveness, yielding accurate results in line with traditional surveying methods used in robotics.

Social media platforms have significantly influenced the dissemination of information, including the spread of misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines via Twitter dialogues. To counter this issue, our study focuses on identifying acceptances or rejections of such misinformation in Twitter conversations. We developed an original dataset consisting of 856 dialogue sentences and secured the approval of an ethics review board. Furthermore, we proposed and implemented a novel neural network architecture, the Dialogue Misinformation Detector (DMID), to address this task. By comparing DMID with various pre-trained language models and human performance, we found that DMID achieved superior results, with a 44% higher accuracy in recognizing rejection sentences and a 219% higher accuracy in recognizing acceptance sentences compared to the best-performing language model.

A novel attosecond pulse drive laser system utilizing a robust-field coherent pulse amplification technique is proposed, which leverages a highly intense, parabolic, laser pulse to generate isolated attosecond pulses through interaction with an atomic target. Unlike existing approaches based on few-cycle pulses, our method can be accurately simulated using a framework that considers the laser pulse's spatial intensity, enabling broader applications and easier implementation. We demonstrate the attosecond pulse generation in neon and argon using a laser pulse with a specific temporal profile, which can be achieved experimentally using a spatial filter and a gas-cell setup.

Recent discoveries by the Zwicky Transient Facility and other researchers suggest that some nearby young stars may have multiple companion planets or objects similar to those found in the Algol AB system. To verify these findings, we conducted a detailed analysis of images from decades past. Our examination of data from 2000 to 2019 showed that allegedly new companions around stars like Algol are actually faint moving stars or background objects. Therefore, it is unlikely that the objects initially identified as new planetary systems are actually present.

We demonstrate a proof of a newly established result that shows for a specific class of initial conditions near a particular equilibrium, a corresponding solution to the nonlinear Schrödinger equation will undergo an explosive outcome. This particular equilibrium, denoted by $q$, represents a standing wave that occurs in the region outside a convex obstacle. This explosive outcome occurs when a specified condition, related to a quantity called $\gamma$, is greater than a certain value, approximately 3/2. Additionally, our methods involve the analysis of a specific equation, referred to as the "energy equation," which is derived from a branch of solutions, denoted as $u(t,\cdot)$, in the $H^2$ space.

One key limitation of traditional physics-based modeling is its inability to accurately represent bridges and boundaries between disparate data points. To address this, we developed the RANG method, a versatile solution for implementing adaptive grid density. The RANG method is based on the residual between adjacent data points and its norm, and thus can be applied within the framework of Physics-Informed Neural Networks. We evaluated the effectiveness of the RANG method on three complex regression tasks: approximating the Robin boundary condition, simulating a heat transfer with a moving boundary, and modeling a moving interface. Our results show that the RANG method can significantly reduce the error and enable INF training.

This study examines the behavior of ferroelectric FETs using a simulation tool that accounts for the multiple domains and charges within the ferroelectric material. We investigate how the adverse capacitance, which causes signal delay and loss, arises due to the domain walls between adjacent ferroelectric domains. Furthermore, we identify the underlying physical mechanisms contributing to adverse capacitance and explore the impact of various parameters, such as domain wall mobility and electrostatic interactions, on this phenomenon. Our simulations reveal that the adverse capacitance can be significantly reduced by preventing domain walls from shifting, which is achievable through the use of a thin insulating channel and a high work function gate material. We also investigate the impact of various ferroelectric materials on adverse capacitance and find that the properties of these materials have a limited effect on this issue, whereas the adverse capacitance can still be eliminated by designing the device appropriately.

The growing freight sector is driven by expanding e-commerce, which poses complex management challenges. To address these issues, a freight system component known as a freight ecosystem, which comprises interconnected companies, has been defined. Freight ecosystem security can be enhanced by identifying and mitigating vulnerabilities. To evaluate the effectiveness of potential countermeasures, a weakness propagation analysis is performed. This paper presents the development of a freight ecosystem dependency-weakness knowledge graph and the results of a propagation study. A novel algorithm is proposed to construct the graph, which helps in understanding the structure of the freight ecosystem and the impact of disturbances. A simulation using real freight data demonstrated the feasibility of the approach and identified key applications.

This study examines the irreducibility of the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation with pure jump noise and its implications for stochastic dynamical systems. We have demonstrated that for systems with noise influenced by a L\'evy process and meeting specific regularity requirements, the associated Markov process is irreducible, provided these noise effects have a significant impact at the system's boundaries. Additionally, our research has significant applications in the study of non-autonomous stochastic dynamical systems and transport theory.

The power graph of a group consists of elements raised to various powers, while the genus of a group refers to the least number of prime factors in its power graph's vertices. Our investigation focuses on the genus of finite nilpotent groups and establishes an upper limit on the genus based on the rank of the group and a specific constant. Moreover, using this constant, we can derive a related limit on the degree of the power graph.

SHADOW will be a highly advanced hadron spectrometer at the CERN SPS and RHIC facilities, as well as a portable device for studying cosmic ray phenomena, with the capability to be stationed at remote locations with minimal access. Its complex design will incorporate an array of cutting-edge detectors to monitor a broad range of particle interactions, with a focus on observing forward particle production, cosmic ray showers, and cosmic radiation at ground level. By integrating a 2.5 Tm long, 9 x 9 m2 surface detector system and a 11 x 11 m2, 2.5 Tm long, 2-layered tracking system with state-of-the-art silicon detectors, SHADOW will possess unparalleled detection capabilities. With its versatile design and adaptability to various experimental setups, SHADOW will have numerous applications in both terrestrial and space-based research, including studying cosmic ray physics, the El'ektroMagnetik Svet (EMF) effect, and air shower physics at ground level.

Inspired by the success of transform-based techniques in transforming data and enhancing its utility, we have created Orientation Convolutive Networks (OCNs). These unique neural networks use orientation-based convolutional layers that utilize a directional filter bank to extract significant features from orientation-sensitive information in images. Unlike regular convolutional networks, which only utilize a limited number of predefined filters, OCNs utilize a varying number of directional filters for a more comprehensive data extraction. We have tested the effectiveness of OCNs in various applications, including directional image recognition and orientation-sensitive image classification, achieving remarkable results in comparison to conventional convolutional networks. Additionally, we have developed a simplified version of OCN, Reduced-Parameter Orientation Convolutive Networks (RPCNs), which significantly reduces the number of network parameters while maintaining its performance.

This paper conducts a comprehensive investigation into graph convolutional networks' functionality in point cloud representation and learning. We identify a critical issue in existing graph convolutional networks, which involves a mismatch between the spatial organization of point clouds and the randomly initialized graph topology. To address this, we propose two effective methods to enhance the representation of point clouds and improve the stability of graph convolutional networks. The first method involves utilizing mean coordinates for graph node initialization, while the second method involves introducing an edge prediction module. By combining these two approaches, we significantly enhance the representation of point clouds and achieve significant improvements in the field of point cloud learning as a whole. Our proposed network, called P2G, consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in 3D object classification, segmentation, and retrieval, showcasing its flexibility and superiority.

Unwanted backdoor attacks targeting deep neural networks have emerged as a significant concern in machine learning. The traditional approach to detecting these backdoors involves incorporating trigger patterns in the activation maps produced by the model, which can lead to inaccurate results if the target is obscured or has a different form. To address this limitation, we introduce a semantic Trojan attack that executes without the need for a host model. Our method allows for the model's base architecture and base activations to be chosen independently, giving us more freedom in design. We also propose an efficient detection system that is less computationally intensive and less prone to false positives. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this semantic Trojan attack and our detection method on various network architectures and activation functions.

We've enhanced the Magellan IMACS RISE (High-Resolution Integral-Field Spectrograph) module, a spatially sensitive instrument that's a part of the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. This upgrade empowers users to select a specific area of interest in the telescope's field of view and collect spectral data from up to 20 distinct objects within a ~20 arcsecond field, translating to a spatial resolution of ~4000 Da or ~270000 Da without the filter. The process involves a CCD with 2048x4096 pixels that's split into two sections, with the ability to choose from 13 different wavelength ranges using a dichroic filter. The Magellan IMACS RISE instrument is now available for public use, and we present the results of an internal validation test.

We have computed the 1S0 fusion cross-sections for colliding ${}^{12}$C ions across a wide range of energies, from 350 to 550 nanobarns, with the aim of resolving a long-standing disagreement between measured values and calculated results using the nuclear physics code CODEYORPHE. Our analysis reveals that the measured and calculated cross-sections exhibit similar energy patterns but with an approximate 2.6 times discrepancy at each energy point. This difference may be attributed to the impact of non-equilibrium neutron-hole configurations in the ${}^{12}$C ground state, which could be explored in future research. Additionally, we have examined the potential of enhancing the Trojan horse technique accuracy by utilizing THRESH, a code developed to analyze experimental data, to analyze three-body reactions. Application of this code to our specific problem is, however, complicated due to computational difficulties associated with the integration of CODEYORPHE and THRESH, as well as the requirement for the ${}^{12}$C ground state wave function, which is not readily available.

A crucial factor in understanding the diversity and and evolution of planetary systems lies in the differences in interior compositions of the planets within those systems. By analyzing the chemical abundance of refractory elements in a star's atmosphere, researchers can infer the types of elements present in a solidified version of that planet. In this study, we utilized a comprehensive approach to determine the interior compositions of exoplanets similar to those found on Kepler-10 and Kepler-10b by creating detailed models of the star and its refractory elements. This required accounting for uncertainties in the star's properties and atmospheric abundance, as well as various processes that could affect planetary accretion and evolution. In our simulations, the resulting compositions of the planets varied significantly due to factors like star evolution and atmospheric mixing. For example, Kepler-10's planets are predicted to have a higher Si/O ratio in their atmospheres than Kepler-10b, potentially due to the effects of star wind and planetary mass. In terms of planetary building, our results indicate that most of the Si and Mg in a planet's core would need to be compensated by a similar amount of Fe. This could pose a challenge for theories of planetary accretion, as it may require the core to be composed of Fe alone. In contrast, a planet with a silicate-rich core could accommodate these elemental ratios with ease. In the context of exoplanets with properties similar to those of Earth, our results suggest that a silicate-rich core is a plausible possibility for

Deep learning-based wireless localization has shown significant potential
in Channel State Information (CSI) data utilization for accurate room
coordinates estimation. However, the conventional deep learning methods used
for CSI utilization overlook the sequential dependencies within CSI sequences.
Our proposed solution leverages the Attention Mechanism to capture these
sequential dependencies in CSI data. As a result, our attention-based model
outperforms the traditional deep learning methods without additional complexity.
Moreover, our model boasts enhanced flexibility by allowing the extraction
of varying sequence lengths from raw CSI without needing manual segmentation.
Extensive experiments are conducted with diverse indoor CSI data, yielding
remarkable results that include an $85\%$ increase in accuracy over the baseline
models.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logics by linking their structural components to topological properties. We utilize a novel extension of Kripke models based on pretopological structures, which incorporates both topological and order structures within a unified framework. We demonstrate how the standard semantic ingredients in modal logics (possible worlds, relations, and valuations) map onto the fundamental components of this structural framework, thereby establishing a direct connection between the two. As a result, we show that the traditional meanings of the box and diamond operators can be seen as induced by the topological structures in terms of closure and openness. Furthermore, we outline a proof system that mirrors the modal logic semantics, employing rules that correspond to the topological properties of intersection, union, closure, and openness.

Bipartite graphs that consist of a pair of disjoint vertex sets, along with edges connecting these vertices, serve as fundamental structures in various graph theory applications. Researchers have proposed an enhanced version of this basic graph structure - the cubic bipartite edge-tinted graph - by incorporating edge colors to distinguish between pairs of vertices, thereby advancing the study of bipartite graphs. Specifically, edge-tinting allows researchers to explore the properties of bipartite graphs by targeting the threshold value at which a given property appears in this enhanced graph structure. Notably, researchers have established that the edge-tinting technique can facilitate a detailed analysis of the rapid mixing phenomenon in bipartite graphs. In this study, we present a counterexample - a specific cubic bipartite graph that exhibits extremely slow mixing - with the aim of understanding how edge-tinting can aid in identifying a threshold value for this mixing property.

This paper explores the minimum threshold of a given function on a Hamming graph, constrained by its spectral properties. Our investigation focuses on a linear function of degree d and an arbitrary vector $\boldsymbol{r}$, which is not orthogonal to the standard basis vector $\boldsymbol{r}_d$. We establish that the minimum threshold for this function is $\Theta\left(\sum_{i=0}^{d-1} \frac{1}{p_i} \right)$. Additionally, if $p_d \gg \sum_{i=0}^{d-1} p_i$, then the minimum threshold is $\Theta\left( \frac{1}{p_d^{1/2}} \right)$. Our results are also applicable to a nonlinear function, specifically $\ell_2$-norm, and yield similar outcomes.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. ShinyCOPASI provides access to the same features as COPASI, including visualizing models, tracking numerical variable values over time, and performing sensitivity analysis. We successfully tested ShinyCOPASIs performance using large models and found that it accurately mirrors COPASI's results. By utilizing ShinyCOPASI, users can easily collaborate, share models and results, and access their models from anywhere, at any time.

Machine learning's extensive applications in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics fields are well-documented but often understated.  Ambiguity in data however poses a significant obstacle to these models.  Not only does uncertainty affect their performance but it also originates from multiple distinct sources.  To address this challenge, scientists and engineers need to 1) detect ambiguity, 2) gauge its magnitude, and 3) develop strategies to mitigate its impact.  This study reviews methods for quantifying ambiguity across various domains, and in conjunction with uncertainty estimation, these metrics inform learning procedures.  To facilitate cross-disciplinary collaboration, we have developed a comprehensive toolkit that harmonizes disparate notions of ambiguity and uncertainty, enabling reproducibility and benchmarking across different datasets and learning algorithms.

We are examining the von Neumann algebra generated by the central type functions on a compact quantum group, $C_{\Phi}^{*}(\mathbb{G})$, and its subalgebra comprised of type $II_{1}$ functions. We have identified a specific *-algebra, $\mathscr{A}_{\Phi}$, whose closure within $C_{\Phi}^{*}(\mathbb{G})$ corresponds to the type $II_{1}$ functions, and found that $\mathscr{A}_{\Phi}$ is densely embedded and diffeomorphic to the algebra of smooth central type functions, $\mathscr{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{G})$, equipped with the compact quantum group action, $\Phi$.

When dealing with significant Markov decision processes (MDPs), a crucial computational challenge arises from optimizing dynamic programming's value function, particularly the Q-function. The problem is the large dimensionality of the Q-function matrix, which hinders its efficient computation via iterative methods like the power iteration. Our proposed solution, Precision Iteration, leverages the GMRES algorithm to circumvent storage issues related to large matrices. Although effective, this method lacks a reliable estimate of the optimal action, which is crucial in decision-making contexts. To address this concern, we developed the Imprecise GMRES iteration (IGM) algorithm. IGM combines two iterations: a search direction computed via GMRES, and an economical step that minimizes noise and amplification of small errors, all within the quadratic cone. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that IGM remains stable and converges to the optimal policy, and our numerical experiments validate its superior performance in large-scale MDPs.

Let $D$ be a weighted directed graph and $R$ the underlying ring with vertex sets, defined using a labelling function $\phi$. The edge ideal $I(D)$ is an affine algebra ideal, and our objective is to determine when a power of $I(D)$ equals a higher power of the ideal, specifically whether $I^{2k+1}(D)=I^{2k+2}(D)$. Our investigation includes two main cases. Firstly, we examine the scenario where the graph $D$ has a spanning tree with no directed cycles, and in this context, we demonstrate that $I^{2k+1}(D)=I^{2k+2}(D)$ if and only if $k=0$. Secondly, we consider the scenario where the graph $D$ contains a cycle, and in this context, we find that $I^{2k+1}(D)=I^{2k+2}(D)$ if and only if $k=0$. Furthermore, for a specific type of edge ideal, known as the ideal of a linearly ordered set of positive integers, we show that $I^{2k+1}(D)=I^{2k+2}(D)$ if and only if $k=0$.

To accurately model the progression of a disease, computer simulations that rely on statistical models based on model-based Bayesian analysis may be necessary. However, these simulations often involve time series data, which can be restricted by small sample sizes and the presence of missing values. A key challenge arises from the inverse problem that must be addressed: how to interpret simulated outcomes back into feasible physical parameters. A proposed method addresses this inverse problem by developing a multiple contour estimation technique that can handle multiple local extrema and leverage posterior distribution information from the Bayesian analysis. This approach is then demonstrated through its application to a lung disease simulation, which showcases its ability to accurately determine the underlying model parameters even with limited data.

This research explores the potential of regional queries in enhancing resilient machine learning in decentralized settings. We assess the performance of an agent using only nearby agents' queries or exclusive access to global information. Unlike existing studies, which often rely on simplified environments, our experiments thoroughly evaluate the performance in a diverse range of scenarios. The results indicate that regional queries can significantly enhance the agent's response when operating in a query-exclusive or information-exclusive environment. However, in situations where both global and regional information are accessible, the agent's performance does not significantly benefit from regional queries.

High-energy partons propagating through the quark-gluon plasma may have their fragmentation altered by interactions with the plasma. To understand this, researchers compared jet fragmentation in Pb+Pb and pp collisions, utilizing isolated photons as reference points. They analyzed charged-particle spectra within these jets, finding that, relative to pp collisions, Pb+Pb collisions exhibit a decrease in long-distance, jet-periphery regions and a shift in jet-core regions. Additionally, researchers observed changes in jet fragmentation in Pb+Pb collisions that depend on the orientation of the collision relative to the collision axis.

Recent research involving Shintaroh Suzuki, Tsukasa Nakamura and Yuya Yamazoe yielded a novel combinatorial identity, which has since been linked to an Ap\'{e}ry-type sequence with distinct index parity. This paper expands upon the given identity, exploring variants with alternate index parity. One such extension was found to correlate with a colored multiple zeta function, specifically of type $4$.

In 2020, an unusual brown dwarf was identified by the community on Twitter, generating more than 1,000 posts within two weeks. This brown dwarf, named WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, is characterized by a unique red color and exhibits a significant proper motion of 11.6 arcseconds per year, making it one of the moving objects in the All-Sky Automated Survey for a drownded object (ASAS-SN) with the highest proper motion. It is also visible to the naked eye with a visual magnitude of approximately 10.5 and is located at a low Galactic latitude of 5.03 degrees. This object is part of a group of fast-moving and low-mass objects that are visible to the naked eye, with only a few examples in the solar neighborhood including a white dwarf, a brown dwarf, and two L and T dwarfs.

This study provides initial data on the production rates of various light hadrons in Xe-Xe collisions at an energy of 5.44 TeV. The data were generated by the ALICE detector at the LHC using a technique that corrects for biases associated with measurement limitations. The research offers a comprehensive exploration of the production patterns for several light hadrons, including simplified representations and intricate simulations, spanning a broad range of energies from a few GeV to over 10 TeV. The results from both experimental measurements and complex simulations reveal significant agreement in the medium-energy region but show a notable disparity at lower energies, suggesting that the interactions between hadrons and the dense QCD medium play a crucial role in this phenomenon.

I introduce an effective technique for evolving parton distribution functions at a specific scale, taking into account higher-order corrections that have been omitted. This method is heavily dependent on the properties of the QCD interaction and is therefore influenced by the phase shift caused by the strong interaction. I provide a mathematical framework that allows me to derive an effective evolution operator at a given scale, incorporating higher-order corrections through a perturbation series. This approach is analogous to a common technique used in condensed matter physics, where a low-frequency approximation is used to obtain a effective description of a system's behavior.

For future lunar and Mars settlements, developing and implementing suitable construction materials from local resources is essential.
Our investigation focused on molding, heating, and characterizing both lunar and Martian samples from NASA's planetary materials collection to determine their mechanical and microstructural properties.
The primary materials analyzed were northern Martian and certified lunar regolith samples.
Both sets of samples were subjected to 0.05 TPa compressive stress in a compression test and X-ray computed tomography was used to examine their internal structures after being heated to 873 K in an argon atmosphere.
The results showed that the compressive strength of both Martian and lunar regolith samples ranged from 0.15 to 0.30 MPa, with the internal structures exhibiting complex patterns.
The effects of sintering heat on the samples' microstructures and mechanical properties were also discussed.

The dynamics of a liquid layer on a fibre initially appear to be governed by the Rayleigh-Plateau instability, causing the liquid to break up into discrete droplets. However, if the liquid and fibre surface are not perfectly bonded, allowing for some degree of slippage, the dynamics change significantly. Even at very small levels of slippage, the liquid breakup process is altered, potentially allowing the formation of droplets on the fibre surface. We have developed a theoretical model that accounts for the effects of slippage and fluid non-linearity, predicting a new type of droplet morphology. Our findings also suggest the possibility of fibre-based materials with tailored pore sizes.

We use a sample of 254 galaxies from a study by Alberts et al. (2017) to compare two methods of estimating star formation rates.
