One method involves analyzing the properties of emission lines through photoionization and collisional excitation, while the other method involves fitting a spectral energy distribution using templates and derives an effective age for the continuum. Our analysis reveals a strong correlation between the two approaches, but with the template-based method generally indicating lower rates of star formation. Notably, the template-based rates are lower than rates derived from emission line strength at redshifts of 2.3 and above, but similar to those at redshifts of 0.64. We attribute the discrepancy between the two approaches to the dominance of old stars in the template-based model of galaxy broadband spectra, as confirmed by a strong correlation between effective ages and redshifts.

This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a significant subset of the type $II$ quantum subgroups within the realm of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$. Part one focuses on identifying some of these subgroups by examining regional bases within the central extensions of the Weyl modules $V(\lambda)$. By identifying regional bases, we are able to describe the action of certain quantum subgroups and establish connections between these subgroups and existing characters from the representation theory of type $I$ quantum subgroups. Notably, regional bases enable us to characterize the irreducible characters within the central extensions of the Weyl modules $V(\lambda)$.

Our proposed method acknowledges the vast influence of social media and online content in shaping modern society, leading to the widespread dissemination of information. To date, research has primarily focused on the rapid spread of a single idea, but our approach aims to simulate and understand the global diffusion of a wide range of concepts, facilitating the exploration of their collective impact. To achieve this, we developed an iterative process combining the principles of social learning and the mechanics of online interaction, demonstrated through a detailed numerical example.

This work addresses the problem of recognizing mathematical expressions handwritten on a paper by paper-based sensors, by converting raw data into a Universal Pen Format (UPF) and transforming it into a Symbol String. A novel approach, the Advanced Symbol String Technique (ASST), is introduced to distinguish between identical symbols and varying handwriting styles. A dataset, the Mathematical Expression Dataset (MED), is developed to evaluate the effectiveness of this method. Experimental results demonstrate that ASST outperforms existing methods on the MED dataset, achieving a recognition accuracy of 93.98% and showcasing great potential for real-world applications.

This research develops an innovative approach to generating synthetic speech at various lengths using a non-statistical method. Unlike previous studies, which relied on probabilistic models, our technique employs median-based interpolation to create desired speech duration. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through experiments using speech modification manipulation, which targets a single spectral feature while preserving the other characteristics. The results of our study reveal that this method produces high-quality speech with minimal artifacts, and its performance is comparable to that of probabilistic methods.

Species distribution analysis, a crucial field in ecology, uses occupancy models to understand where species are found. These models simulate field observations, even when data is missing or incomplete. We created spOccupancy for building and evaluating single-species, combined species, and joint species occupancy models that take into account spatial relationships and multiple survey periods. This toolkit uses Stan for efficient model computation, allowing users to specify custom prior distributions. A range of diagnostics and prediction tools are also included to support model interpretation and analysis.

Skin cancer is the most prevalent type of cancer in the United States, with a growing incidence rate influenced by environmental and lifestyle factors. Early detection is crucial for a high success rate, with the need to adapt traditional training methods to incorporate medical professionals in educating AI models. Skincare, an innovative deep learning system, is designed to interact with dermatologists for malignant melanoma and other skin lesion identification. By integrating dermatological expertise, Skincare enhances its accuracy in classifying lesion characteristics and characteristics relevant to diagnosis. Compared to non-dermatologically trained models, Skincare demonstrates superior performance in producing relevant and informative results for human evaluation, highlighting the benefits of collaborative AI systems in medical applications.

To capture the underlying structure of type Ia supernovae spectra across time,
we utilize a stochastic variational autoencoder. This approach addresses the
challenges posed by noisy and highly variable data by modeling the intricate
temporal relationships within supernova evolution. The desired temporal framework
is embedded in the latent space of the stochastic autoencoder, allowing us to
generate time-series data and reconstruct the spectral phases of a supernova,
even when only the reddest phase is observed. Our findings demonstrate that the
latent space effectively encodes the spectral development of a supernova, and
the associated prior distribution represents typical phase-to-phase variations.
Furthermore, we find that SNe Ia with similar redshifts and z-magnifications are
grouped in the latent space.

The formation of galaxies in the early universe is significantly influenced by the process of galaxy interaction and merger. These events release large amounts of energy and dust, which are essential for the development of galaxies through the absorption and re-emission of light. A recent Hubble study caught a rare instance of a galaxy in the act of egress from a merged galaxy (a merger event witnessed ~100 million years earlier). This unique observation offers insights into the role of dust in galaxies. For the purpose of this study, researchers employed radiation transfer modeling to simulate dust behavior under various radiation conditions. By adjusting model parameters and considering neutral gas distribution, they successfully replicate key observed features, including continuum spectra and absorption lines at specific wavelengths. Notably, models indicating a relatively small and compact dust distribution align with expectations, while gas and dust present in the galaxy are observed to be misaligned, a characteristic observed in galaxies undergoing egress.

We examine the behavior of spherical bodies descending through a turbulent environment. The particles influence the surrounding fluid, causing it to expand and alter the characteristics of the wake. We derived equations for the fluid's velocity and pressure in this modified system, and verified that, under certain conditions, our findings coincide with those from previous studies. Additionally, we investigated how the fluid's flow impacts the particles, calculating their acceleration and evaluating the dynamics of their motion. Our analysis covers a broad range of scenarios, including cases where the fluid's flow slows down as it moves further away from the plume's center and those with constant horizontal flow rates.

For understanding the spread of epidemics, we consider a model on complex network structures, specifically hypergraphs, where a disease can spread from one infected individual to multiple susceptible ones at once. A mathematical approach called the "mean-field approximation" allows us to analyze this phenomenon and develop a framework for determining the threshold values that dictate whether an outbreak occurs. We also investigate the limits of this approximation and discover an intricate relationship between the network's underlying structure and the rates of disease transmission and recovery. These findings enable the identification of distinct spectral characteristics within the transmission matrix, influencing the outcome of an epidemic. Numerical simulations on various hypergraph examples, including a random model, demonstrate the efficacy of our method.

Using a high-level approach, we've analyzed the magnetic properties of the 2D ferromagnet CrI3 bilayer and found that its magnetic structure exhibits unusual features. Despite being centrosymmetric, the material exhibits a unique spin profile with components in multiple directions. Through calculations, we identified several mechanisms contributing to the spin profile, including an imbalance of magnetic interactions, a non-rashba effect due to lattice distortion, and a rashba effect originating from atomic structure. We've also observed that applying external pressure can modify the spin profile. Our research provides a theoretical basis for understanding the unique magnetic properties of CrI3 bilayer and related materials.

Low-energy, solar-type rotators are experiencing extensive study, particularly through Kepler mission data, which has revealed extensive samples of such stars. Recent dynamo simulations have focused on producing ring-like patterns, similar to those observed on the Sun and in asteroseismic data. This research builds upon that concept by investigating how altering the Sun's unusual rotation rate, known as anti-solar differential rotation, affects dynamo simulations. We utilized the AURA framework to run extensive simulations of low-energy, solar-type rotators with varying levels of activity and anti-solar differential rotation. Our results show that decreasing the Sun's rotation rate significantly impacts the strength and distribution of magnetic activity throughout the stellar surface. Specifically, this modification leads to increased low-frequency and high-frequency activity, while pushing intermediate frequencies downward in the power spectrum. We discovered that combining anti-solar differential rotation with weak helical turbulence results in reduced toroidal magnetic field strength, while allowing for the development of large-scale poloidal magnetic fields. Ultimately, we found that incorporating anti-solar differential rotation into solar-type dynamos may explain the observed low levels of activity and the lack of cyclic behavior in such stars, as well as potentially accounting for low-frequency variability.

We introduce a versatile deep learning approach that integrates various computer vision techniques in a unified framework. Our method, called the Universal K-fan network (UKN), employs a modular architecture consisting of multiple stages, each comprising a feature extraction module, a classification module, a loss function, and an optimizer. By selecting only the relevant parameters, we can implement UKN as a compact, efficient model that achieves state-of-the-art results for multiple vision tasks. Our experiments demonstrate the UKN's capability to resolve 11 key problems, such as object classification, detection, segmentation, generation, and reinforcement learning-based tasks, across three datasets (CIFAR10, ImageNet, and COCO). Furthermore, our proposed framework outperforms existing solutions in a large-scale benchmark test, showcasing its versatility and computational efficiency.

McMini, a McMillan-style model verifier for multithreaded programs, uses a Davis Putnam style model-based approach that involves algorithmic and data structure modifications to enhance performance. This enhanced model, which handles predicate abstraction and CLP, exhibits an improvement in McMillan's original model and also displays a more efficient progression of models, with a time complexity of O(n*m) as opposed to O(n*m^2).

The widespread circulation of false information through social media is an ongoing issue, with significant repercussions on real-world events. Amidst this concern, messaging apps have emerged as another significant spread channel of misinformation. This study evaluates the impact of a feature limiting message forwarding on one such app, WhatsApp, in an effort to curb the spread of false information among users. We examined this strategy by analyzing conversations involving users who interacted with misinformation, surveying users and examining actual messages sent on WhatsApp in Peru and Colombia. The results indicate that limiting message forwarding neither completely eradicates misinformation nor effectively hinders its transmission. Conversely, the feature appears to primarily restrict transmission among closest social circles, with little effect on larger groups. Conversely, removing the forwarding limit actually increased users' exposure to misinformation in some cases. Ultimately, we propose that limiting message forwarding be complemented by a more comprehensive strategy addressing the root cause of misinformation transmission, which we outline.

We model a population using a general branching process, where each individual gives rise to a random number of offspring according to a specific distribution. This population's genetic makeup is based on a simple model, where individuals can possess the same allele. We then establish a mathematical framework to determine the likely frequency distribution of different alleles within this population, assuming an infinite number of generations. This analysis reveals that, under a specific condition, the frequency distribution of alleles approximates a specific pattern, given enough generations, and is characterized by a specific function. We also provide estimates of the likelihood and standard deviation of an allele's frequency at a given generation.

Activation functions play a crucial role in improving neural network performance; however, their effectiveness in enhancing anti-spoofing capabilities remains unknown. Inspired by the concept of vigilance in security, we introduce the Vigilant activation function, which leverages anomaly detection to monitor and adjust activation values, thereby preventing spoofing attempts. Experiments conducted on deep neural network-based anti-spoofing systems revealed that systems utilizing the Vigilant activation function exhibited improved EER and AUC scores compared to standard ReLU and Leaky ReLU activation functions.

Supergravity, a unification of physics, when applied to inflationary models, requires a more accurate approach due to vanishing spinors. Traditional field theory methods are insufficient in this scenario. We develop a new approach, leveraging the supersymmetric lemma, to formulate an efficient gauge-invariant action for these models. This novel action enables a direct comparison with S-matrix elements, even in the absence of a manifold. We apply this method to two locally supersymmetric inflationary models, providing a clearer understanding of their dynamics.

We examine the phenomenon of asymmetry in photon pair correlations, which is typically associated with fourth-order coherence. Our analysis begins by identifying a general framework for studying asymmetry in systems that follow a $N$-th order coherence pattern. By applying our framework to study a specific, well-documented scenario - an ensemble of two-level atoms - we reveal that asymmetry in photon pair correlations arises due to differences in the atomic states contributing to the correlation function. These disparities are rooted in the on-demand nature of single-atom transitions, which leads to a distinct, predictable pattern in apparent randomness.

Receiving information in the terahertz frequency range offers numerous benefits, 
including extremely fast data transfer rates and highly sensitive material 
detection capabilities. Despite its advantages, working with terahertz waves 
presented significant difficulties due to old and limited technology availability. 
A new technique has been developed to visually inspect terahertz waves without 
having to physically be on the microwave circuit itself. This technique uses 
surface terahertz waves that are confined and near-total absorption, making it 
possible to precisely measure electromagnetic field strengths. By applying this 
 Technique to a lumped circuit, we were able to accurately determine both the 
position and amplitude of the generated terahertz waves.

The Borel sets on the real line form a σ-algebra that generates the σ-algebra of Borel sets when taking the σ-algebra induced by any measure. We are interested in the cardinality of collections of Borel subsets that partition the real line, and we examine the least possible cardinality for such collections, considering different families of Borel sets, including those generated by different types of topological properties.

This study examines the impact of novel investment tactics on existing strategies in a dynamic environment. We simulate multiple scenarios of novel tactics emerging at different times and simulate agent-based investment strategies, including a naive strategy for comparison. The analysis under novel conditions reveals varying levels of performance for each strategy, with significantly decreased naive strategy outcomes when confronted with multiple novel tactics. However, an interesting finding emerges when a novel tactic is introduced at a slower pace: the naive strategy experiences increased returns, outperforming the specialized strategies. This phenomenon is attributed to the timing of novel tactic adoption by the agent, which differs from optimal timing calculated through backtesting.

A growing number of network service providers are being targeted by malicious attackers, with the consequence being significant financial losses in the US, with projected losses rising to $6 billion by the end of 2023. To combat these attacks, network protection monitoring (NPM) is being utilized by service providers to detect and prevent assaults in real-time, with the additional benefit of enabling law enforcement agencies to investigate crimes more effectively. However, the use of NPM is primarily based on open-source tools that encrypt traffic, posing a challenge for assault detection since the current methods cannot identify which type of assault has occurred when traffic is encrypted. A new technique, known as dynamic protocol identification (DPI), has been proposed to address this issue by identifying the encryption method used on a given network. Unfortunately, the current implementation of DPI is flawed and can be manipulated, which has significant implications for its potential misuse. This research paper presents an innovative approach, using a cryptanalytic technique to deceive the DPI algorithm and determine the type of encryption used on a given network, even when no data is available for analysis.

Electrostatic gating limits the flow of electrons, but what about magnetic fluctuations?  We simulate how a nearby superconductor can "gates" magnons, the quasi-particles resulting from these fluctuations, using a two-dimensional Hubbard model.  By applying a uniform magnetic field, we observe the system's magnetic structure and find that the superconductor's presence causes magnon spectral weight to shift away from the localized, strongly coupled region near the Fermi level towards higher energy levels, where it becomes less affected by the magnetic field, thus reducing the impact of the magnons on the system's magnetic properties.  This phenomenon is most noticeable when the superconductor's proximity to the other material is closest, with notable effects on both the upper and lower Hubbard bands, indicating that the superconductor's influence extends beyond just the doped region, potentially allowing for novel applications of the "gating" effect, such as in spin machines.

This study focuses on using pre-trained models and knowledge acquired from prior tasks to classify novel audio scenes without any associated labels. We draw inspiration from established research in visual zero-shot learning and apply it to the development of a unified framework for zero-shot, distributed, deep neural network-based acoustic scene classification. Our proposed framework relies on a two-part model that comprises a universal, pre-trained feature extractor and class-dependent projection modules, which are trained end-to-end using data from established classes. We then evaluate the effectiveness of this framework on a dataset that includes supplementary material beyond the initial training set. Our results indicate that this approach surpasses a strong baseline by successfully identifying novel classes with minimal data from multiple sources.

Achieving high-dimensional encoded quantum systems is crucial for enhancing quantum communication security, but creating and evaluating multi-dimensional correlated states like the high-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state remains a complex task. Given the limitations of current measurement methods, which can't always directly detect these states in high-dimensional spaces, we propose a protocol using the quantum field of an optical fiber to measure the GHZ state in a multi-dimensional space. The proposed protocol enhances the accuracy of determining correlation in high-dimensional encoded systems by combining both space and frequency dimensions. The proposed method proves to be an efficient way to assess high-dimensional correlated states.

This research focuses on optimizing energy efficiency in a multi-user downlink wireless system, with an intelligent reflecting surface technology being utilized. To efficiently support a varying number of users within a given bandwidth, a novel selective channel assessment algorithm is developed. This algorithm prioritizes users based on signal strength and then allocates resources accordingly. A mathematical model is created to maximize a linear representation of energy efficiency, with the number of users and available frequency blocks taken into consideration. The algorithm's complexity is minimized through a series of simplifications. A computationally efficient and adaptive algorithm is developed, with simulation results demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving optimal performance.

This study analyzes regional online news coverage during the COVID-19 pandemic in the U.S., examining its relationship with case and death rates, as well as audience responses, by leveraging a large dataset and network of online news sources. Our results show that regions with higher COVID-19 activity received more online news coverage and that certain news topics were more prevalent in hard-hit areas. Additionally, our investigation into audience reactions reveals that readers in regions experiencing high COVID-19 activity are more likely to engage with news related to the pandemic, especially if their local authorities have implemented lockdown measures.

A recent area of research in deep neural networks focuses on enhancing the network's memory capacity to support superior performance. Our work builds upon this progress by applying memory-augmented neural networks to count objects in sequences. To evaluate their progression, we developed a novel, consistent dataset featuring increasing object counts within gradually extended sequences. Our results indicate that these models are initially hindered in predicting total counts but ultimately achieve high accuracy with enhanced memory capabilities.

Filter data structures like Bloom and Cuckoo filters use hash functions to determine membership in a set. A negative result indicates the element is not present, but a positive result is inconclusive. In contrast, membership is certain with a positive result but uncertain with a negative result. Building on this concept, xor filters offer more efficient performance than both Bloom and Cuckoo filters for partial set membership queries. Additionally, they consume less space than Bloom filters when used for exact set membership. Our analysis compares the trade-offs among xor, Bloom, and cuckoo filters and explores variants of xor filters that have been optimized through compensation and rehashing.

This talk explores the connections between three related concepts: the topology of certain convex spaces, the analytic structure of K\"ahler spaces, and the geometric properties of projective spaces. We will examine correspondence mechanisms and examine the implications of various notions of homeomorphism, biholomorphic equivalence, and projective equivalence on these three different types of spaces.

A recent study proposes a distinct approach for trend analysis in a trading platform. This method utilizes neural networks to identify patterns in a unique dataset, called AET (average execution time), AE (average price), and EMS (average traded shares), extracted from a sequence of market transactions. This dataset offers a single-dimensional representation of market data, unaffected by fluctuations in time. Two versions of the trend analyzer are presented: one that relies on historical data and market observations, and another that incorporates future knowledge for comparative purposes. Experimental findings, based on analysis of the Bitcoin exchange, demonstrate that both analyzers are capable of identifying trends, although the model with future knowledge is more effective.

This research introduces FLVoogd, a robust and privacy-conscious federated learning framework. Federated learning can be vulnerable to poisoning attacks, which compromise model accuracy or privacy. FLVoogd incorporates two effective techniques to mitigate such threats: (1) accurate gradient estimation, preventing biased model learning, and (2) constant privacy maintenance, upholding users' confidentiality throughout the training process. Both techniques are unprecedently combined in FLVoogd, offering enhanced security and privacy protections for federated learning applications.

Our proposed method successfully transfers autonomous navigation skills from a simulated environment to real-world navigation. To achieve this, we developed a novel image processing technique utilizing edge detection, leveraging the principles of image gradient calculation to bridge the gap between simulated and actual image representations. By converting navigation skills learned in simulation to apply to real-world navigation, we streamlined the autonomous navigation process, ending the need for constant manual supervision.

Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincing deepfakes using fewer media sources and less training data. Despite their advancements, deepfake detection remains a challenging task due to the vast amount of unconstrained video content available. Our research addresses this issue by developing robust and generalizable approaches for deepfake creation and detection that can withstand out-of-distribution inputs. We specifically focus on improving deepfake detection by incorporating a framework that adapts to noise and produces more accurate scores. Furthermore, our novel method surpasses existing state-of-the-art benchmarks, as evidenced by our results on the PG3, FaceForensK, and Celeb-DF datasets.

The composition of approximately one-third of all planets discovered in the Kepler sample remains unknown, with some showing signs of habitability. For the first category of detectable planets, specifically those with masses similar to that of Earth and orbital periods less than 100 days, our model presents a new approach that can predict the mass of a planet's water component using observable ratios of atmospheric silicates to metals. Unlike existing methods, our framework relies on observable features related to the stability of various compounds at high pressures, rather than requiring expensive simulations or specific assumptions about a planet's formation. As a result, our framework can distinguish between different possible iron compounds in a planet's interior, as well as their interaction with atmospheric metals. Additionally, our framework identifies two key features in the observable silicate-metal ratio spectrum that are highly sensitive to a planet with a hidden ocean. These features are a steep increase at low wavelengths and a steep decrease at high wavelengths. The combination of these signatures, along with the silicate-metal ratio, allows us to identify hidden oceans on planets with masses similar to that of Earth.

A spike-based neural network's ability to learn over time is crucial for its long-term information retention and adaptation to changing environments. Both online and offline learning approaches in spike-based neural networks have been explored in previous studies. However, these studies often relied on simplified biological models that ignored certain aspects of real neural behavior. In contrast, our work builds on a more complex model that accounts for real neural dynamics, and we demonstrate its applicability to both offline and real-time online learning in spiking neural networks.

This report outlines the results of the out-of-context language model challenge to date.
Language models are now expected to perform equally well in both controlled and real-world settings.
We note that a substantial gap remains between the capabilities of the top language models and human experts in
non-studied, real-world contexts. 
Our benchmark, consisting of 100 tasks across five domains, has been completed by 16 teams and we observe
that even the most successful models and teams struggle with tasks outside of their trained data.
These challenges highlight the limitations of current language models in understanding context-dependent information
and highlight the need for further model advancements and innovative techniques.

A specific type of chaos expansions, known as generalized polynomial chaos expansions, can effectively approximate certain function classes on diverse random domains. The traditional approach for estimating expansion errors involves comparing approximate and exact function values on separate probability spaces with closely related measures. Alternatively, we will demonstrate that a posteriori error analysis is possible, provided that certain conditions on these measures are met. This alternative approach enables the computation of actual error thresholds in addition to estimating error bounds. To illustrate the proposed method, we will apply it to approximations of random PDE solutions via finite element methods.

In a variety of dynamic systems, changes occur over time that affect partially observable states, and these alterations must be detected and accommodated for in order to make informed decisions. Despite the abundance of classical monitoring techniques for overall systems, they frequently fail to recognize that some states have remained unaltered. Our research focuses on identifying sequential changes in partially observable systems in real-time and providing an adaptive solution that can handle simultaneous system modifications. A real-time algorithm is developed using online statistical methods and linear programming, which accurately detects and separates changing states within a limited number of iterations. Our algorithm is further enhanced by incorporating an adaptive sensitivity analysis that adjusts its parameters according to the availability and quality of observed data. This adaptation prevents over-processing data and over-estimating changes. Our study showcases the performance of this adaptive algorithm through simulations involving a variety of dynamic systems, including a large-scale network of interconnected processes.

We've developed a framework to analyze the evolution of dwarf galaxies through their stellar population's chemical composition and life cycles. This framework combines a chemical evolution model and a Bayesian inference tool to quantify the contributions of supernovae and stellar winds from various star types at different developmental stages. By applying this framework to dwarf galaxies of various masses and metallicity, we identify key patterns in the rates and effects of mass loss and supernovae explosions across space and time. Our analysis suggests that low-mass stars have a mass range of approximately 0.1-0.9 solar masses, and that both low-mass and high-mass stars experience mass loss at different stages of their life cycles. Furthermore, we find that both core collapse and supernovae explosions supernovae have a mass range of approximately 10^5-10^9 solar masses, and that both low-mass and high-mass stars contribute to the metal enrichment at different stages of the galaxy's life cycle.

We define the notion of a homotopy $G$-space for a profinite group $G$ as an honest $G$-space after taking the wrecker completion over $G$. This idea ties in with Barwick and Ganter's homotopy group completion theory. As a result, we introduce the concept of a homotopy action of $G$ on a homotopy $G$-space and establish that a functorial method exists to calculate the homotopy action group $G$ acting on a homotopy $G$-space, which we term the 'true' homotopy action group. Moreover, under mild assumptions, this action is equivalent to the action provided by the Borel functor. This process also enables the derivation of an abstract version of the Borel functor, which we refer to as the homotopy action spectrum. By applying this abstract version to the total homotopy $G$-space, it yields the ordinary homotopy group spectrum. This new spectrum possesses a natural $G$-action, which is true rather than derived through the Borel functor.

Accurate training of machine learning models to extract data from complex documents requires a substantial number of visually rich, well-structured and annotated examples. However, manually creating and grouping these documents with their corresponding extraction layouts proves to be a costly and time-consuming activity, especially when dealing with large datasets. In this research, we explore the potential of adapting a recent text manipulation model to automatically create these necessary datasets by itself, without the need for human intervention. By leveraging this model, we demonstrate a significant reduction in labeling expenses and still achieve comparable results, surpassing our previous approach in fact.

The EuS/InAs interface has been proposed as a promising material for reliable, noise-tolerant spin-orbit qubits. Our study provides a detailed examination of the electronic structure at the interface between InAs (111) and EuS, utilizing density functional theory with a hybrid functional to calculate the electronic framework. By comparing our results with an experimental study, our theoretical findings support the existence of a localized state at the interface, approximately 10 volts below the Fermi level. We also observe that the electronic structure is heavily influenced by the choice of bonding arrangement between the EuS monolayer and the InAs substrate. When the EuS monolayer is bonded to the InAs substrate with a misaligned interface, a significant shift in energy occurs, resulting in a more positive voltage. This bonding configuration is hypothesized to be the most likely arrangement at the interface and may lead to favorable spin properties within the localized state at the interface.

We provide an efficient classification system for subsets of Baire space that can be recognized through a finite series of continuous functions and elementary computations. This classification system is comparative with respect to a specific hierarchy of subsets, which is defined by a particular testing process that builds upon continuous functions. As a result of this classification, we can demonstrate that a particular type of infinite mathematical sequence, known as the Borel sets, is inherently countable. Furthermore, proof of this result also allows us to demonstrate that a different collection of infinite mathematical sequences, known as the analytic sets, is also countably infinite.

Despite recent advances in deep neural networks, the enormous size of them poses significant challenges to training them, including increased computational demands, memory consumption, and difficulties in handling model complexity. Previous studies have attempted to address these issues through pruning, which alleviates these problems after the pruning process is complete. However, pruning often leads to a significant increase in inference time and accuracy degradation due to the re-growth of pruned weights during model refinement. In this study, we introduce ClickTrain, a novel method that combines pruning and efficient training techniques to achieve substantial improvements without compromising model quality. ClickTrain proactively identifies and mitigates weight uncertainties during training, dynamically pruning non-relevant connections and leveraging the remaining parameters to accurately perform classification tasks. Our approach is centered on the principle of architecture preservation – minimizing weight changes while maintaining the overall structure. ClickTrain's continuous monitoring of model complexity during training enables it to adaptively focus on crucial parameters, resulting in a highly accurate and efficient model with near-zero parameters. Our experiments demonstrate that ClickTrain surpasses current pruning and training methods, achieving a remarkable 2x reduction in model size while maintaining 0.00% top-1 error and a 2x decrease in inference time with a Google BERT model.

We examine the full modal functionality version of the calculi in MLL, MLL+, and NL. By fully classifying the axioms for these calculi, we are able to demonstrate the solvability of any given non-distributive lattice equation with modal functions. Additionally, the axioms in these calculi have natural applications in the contexts of category theory and process semantics.

Collisions between neutron stars and black holes emit gravitational waves across a broad spectrum of frequencies, ranging from low frequency GWs detected by ground-based detectors to the high frequency GWs analyzed by detectors in space. The integration of ground-based and orbital detectors enables the comprehensive identification and classification of these GWs throughout their frequency range, covering up to the cut-off frequency (f_max = 2000 Hz) associated with the disintegration of the neutron star. Our approach uses a neural network that can identify and classify these GWs under various conditions, including through noisy signals and across different detector networks combining data from ground-based and space-based detectors. The development of a reliable neural network classifier is crucial for accurately labeling the signals from actual neutron star-black hole collisions, which will facilitate the advancement of astrophysics and understanding neutron star evolution through gravitational wave analysis.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant planet, which orbits around a middle-aged star approximately 5 billion years old called TOI-5542. Located at a distance of about 390 parsecs from Earth, this star is part of a study on an old Jupiter-like planet, which is one of the first of its kind. TOI-5542 hosts a massive planet, which is approximately 1.2 times the size of Jupiter, orbiting the star in a close proximity of about 3.8 days. This planet's characteristics can be compared to those of hot Jupiters, which are in a different stage of their lives, despite being much younger. Interestingly, this planet's size is relatively consistent over time, which is an unusual feature for hot Jupiters. This study provides new insights into a planet's evolution, which challenges existing theories.

In recent years, Markov decision processes (MDPs) with restricted state-action pairs have gained significant attention. These restricted pairs are often based on various criteria such as distance, visibility, and more. The concept of Markov choice procedures (MCPs) has been developed to address this issue, allowing for state-action pair selection in an iterative manner. The main goal of an MCP is to find the most suitable pair at each step, given the constraint of not selecting it again until a certain time period has passed. The time period is determined by a parameter 'k'. The problem of MCP applies across different sectors such as supply chains and public health, where the optimal strategy involves making decisions based on future uncertainties. The MCP is categorized into two types: the first, which involves an exhaustive search (EMCP), and the second, which uses an iterative procedure to update the selection probabilities (IMCP). Theoretical insights into both EMCP and IMCP show that they can be solved efficiently in polynomial time under specific conditions. The main contribution of our research is the development of a primal-dual algorithm for solving the IMCP, particularly when 'k' is relatively small. The proposed algorithm is compared with an iterative expected value approach and is shown to outperform it under certain conditions. The results of our study also shed light on the relationship between 'k' and the optimal value of IMCP. Finally, the computational experiments using a supply chain scenario validate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

This study focuses on the offline handwritten mathematical notation recognition task.
Despite being a crucial component of math education, this task has received relatively
little attention from researchers. To address this gap, we have developed a comprehensive
dataset, MathHandwriteDB, which features real-world handwritten math expressions from
primary and secondary school levels. This dataset boasts diverse math expressions along
with their corresponding labeled transcripts. Moreover, we have crafted a customized
evaluation protocol to accurately assess recognition performance across various math
symbol categories. In addition, we have devised a novel approach, consisting of a complex
network architecture, specifically designed for offline handwritten math recognition.
Our experimental results, obtained using the MathHandwriteDB dataset, demonstrate the
efficacy of our proposed approach and evaluation protocol.

We've established a link between the expansion of sheaf cohomology and the Witten index in supersymmetric quantum mechanics. By demonstrating that they share common underlying principles, such as the Leray model and the superconnection expansion, we show that certain geometric and topological methods apply across diverse contexts. This becomes clear through the comparison of cohomology and Witten index computations for a variety of examples, including a singular vector field on a sphere and a projective bundle over a surface with specific singularities.

This study examines how differences in complex networks affect the development and spread of a spreading process. To address this, a generic model is proposed that analyzes a temporary competition between two distinct processes on a complex network. One process is a spreading phenomenon, whereas the other is a local interaction event triggered by spreading elements. By applying this model to various network structures, it is observed that the ratio of a network's small-world characteristics to its disorder varies significantly. This observation is the foundation for an hypothesis, which is further validated through numerical simulations on both artificial and real-world networks.

Reinforcement learning has gained significant attention in recent years due to its wide range of applications, from game playing to robotic control. The actor-critic method, a type of policy gradient method, is widely employed for its effectiveness. However, one major challenge associated with this method is optimizing the stochastic policy, which is crucial for exploring the environment efficiently. Despite the use of second-order derivatives, exploring the probability distribution of an action variable may not be adequately sampled, particularly at the critical points. In our study, we integrated the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) technique into the actor-critic method to address this issue. The HMC technique draws its inspiration from its high-efficiency counterpart, variational inference, which has been successfully applied to various machine learning tasks. Our research demonstrates that combining the HMC technique with the actor-critic method enhances exploration and significantly improves the learning efficiency. We conducted thorough experiments using both simple toy examples and complex 3D navigation tasks, which consistently showed the combined approach outperformed the traditional actor-critic method.
A concise and straightforward proof is provided for the Twin Prime Congruence, which leads to the Twin Prime Hypothesis as a consequence.

Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) rely on sonar technology to map and navigate underwater environments. Although using multiple sonars can enhance coverage, merging their data is complex. This research presents a novel, straightforward approach for combining sonar data from an array of beams. Unlike existing methods that require significant processing and data analysis, this technique efficiently handles multiple sonar readings by simply overlaying their ranges. Additionally, our approach respects the unique capabilities and limitations of each sonar, accurately accounting for their field of view and resolution. As a result, navigation and planning decisions based on this merged data are informed by a more comprehensive understanding of the surroundings. To demonstrate the efficacy of this method, we have applied it in an underwater simulation scenario and shown that it enables more thorough path planning for an autonomous vehicle.

We've analyzed Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that's notable for its highly elliptical orbit, using its near-infrared reflectance spectrum. This analysis provides key information about the composition and mixing of its bright surface materials, offering insights into its geological and orbital history. Our findings indicate that Nereid's spectrum is best fit by a mixture of water ice with salting or other volatiles, on top of a darker, organic-rich mantle. Two models are presented: a'saltline' model featuring eutectic mixtures of ammonium chloride and water ice, and a 'volatile' model containing methane and ethane ices along with carbon dioxide and water. Both models agree that Nereid's water ice eutectics range from 50 to 70 mole percent and that its total 'dark' fraction is approximately 30 to 40 mole percent. This analysis supports the idea that Nereid's surface is composed of pure water ice only in the polar regions, while the rest is significantly altered by the presence of volatiles. This discovery also suggests that Nereid's highly elliptical orbit may prevent it from reaching the boundary where methane and ethane ices condense, at least 50 K as measured on Saturn's satellite, Phoebe. This analysis further reveals that Nereid's N+2 N2 band feature shows a redshift of 0.5 nm, indicating a temperature of 42 K, and that

Let $\mathcal{R}$ denote the ring of lower triangular $3\times 3$ matrices with integer entries, with a specific property. We study affine and projective surfaces in the affine space of $9$ dimensions, over the field of real numbers, whose equations are defined by the generators of $\mathcal{R}$. These surfaces are then linked to projective lines in the projective space of $8$ dimensions, under certain conditions.

We propose a modified sequence of reals that reinforces Pawlikowski's theorems on the uncountability of $\aleph_1$ and does not rely on large cardinal axioms, unlike previous proofs by Borel and Solovay. This new approach uses an infinite game of Martin's, specifically the auto-homeomorphism of the Cantor space, to establish a fundamental relationship between reals and continuous functions on a specific space.

In the context of dynamic treatment strategies and Bayesian learning, our research focuses on pessimistic approaches that are resilient to uncertainty. Pessimistic approaches are particularly useful because they can withstand ill-conditioned or data-starved examples without being unduly influenced by them. However, these methods are generally applicable only to a limited class of problems involving simple treatment strategies. We have developed a more powerful learning algorithm that can handle complex treatment strategies and is influenced by the long-term effects of past actions through the utilization of a model of the underlying system. We have evaluated our algorithm in both theoretical and practical terms, assessing its ability to adapt to changing environments and comparing it to the performance of alternative strategies in a range of scenarios.

Dualities between category theories of algebraic, topological or analytical nature have been a subject of interest for a while, with connections to homological invariants being particularly noteworthy. This brief discussion aims to highlight some notable dualities and their implications for homological invariants.

A proposed lattice system based on the $E_8$ root system serves as the basis for a discussion about two fundamental concepts: the entanglement and nonlocality of quantum systems, along with their equivalent expression through certain classical systems with multiple valued outcomes. The argument centers around a reformulation of the Mermin lightcone order parameter in lower dimensional lattices, revealing that the principle of nonlocality is an inherent aspect of systems comprising at least two interacting qubits. Conversely, entanglement emerges as a critical aspect of systems with an even number of interacting qubits. In a d-dimensional lattice with a growth rate of qubits, our findings indicate that the rate of entanglement generation outpaces the rate of nonlocality. Finally, we explore the potential for these outcomes in recent experiments utilizing 99Tc+ ions.

Research has demonstrated that exotic condensates can form in specially designed lattice models with multiple-band structures. Focusing on a quantum spin Hall model featuring two coupled bands, we analyzed the behavior of bosonic modes in this system and found that a stable Bose condensate can emerge within one of the bands in the presence of another occupied band. When both bands are occupied to the same degree, a BCS condensate may also appear. We also identify a condition under which both types of condensates can simultaneously occur. Our results indicate that this phenomenon is related to an effective attraction between particles resulting from band mixing, leading to a description of the observed effects within a effective single-band model.

Let $G$ be a connected, compact, locally compact, abelian group of dimension 1. In a joint work with A. N. Starko, we demonstrate that the Fourier transform of $G$ is isomorphic to the character group of a countable, totally ordered group. Furthermore, we establish a generalization of the second part of Universal Polya's theorem, initially proved by I. V. Gurevich in 1936.

In the study of microbial communities, we analyzed presence-absence data from 386 environmental samples, each containing 6660 OTUs. Our approach used a similarity measure called Jaccard index to calculate distances between samples, and several clustering methods were applied with a range of parameters including hierarchical, linkage-based clustering and non-hierarchical techniques like Autoencoder and K-Means. To evaluate the effectiveness of different clustering methods, we used indices such as Calinksi-Hinksley criterion, Rand index and Silhouette width, and also assessed their results visually using a dendrogram and map of clustered samples. Ultimately, the best results were achieved using hierarchical Agglomerative clustering with Ward's method, which showed a significant improvement over other methods and particularly improved classification of samples at depths greater than 10 nm when combined with additional filtering.

Most existing salient object detection methods focus exclusively on using visual information and disregard other potential sources, even if available. To address this, we propose a novel, unified framework that seamlessly integrates features from RGB and depth images. We understand that depth maps can provide valuable information about an image's structure, which in turn aids the identification of the most visually distinctive areas. Our framework consists of three core components: the initial feature extraction, the reciprocal interaction of RGB and depth features, and the differential feature enhancement. By doing so, we are able to accurately locate the most salient areas in images, a skill previously reserved for human observation. Extensive testing using widely-accepted evaluation metrics revealed our method to be highly competitive, surpassing current state-of-the-art approaches in nearly all instances.

This paper reports our results in the 2019 SemEval-Task 6 Subtask A, which involved classifying English tweets into three categories: not aggressive, mildly aggressive, and highly aggressive. Our approach, which combined advancements in NLP with feature engineering, utilized BERT as a text representation model and combined various machine learning classifiers with SVMs to achieve a high micro-average F1 score of 0.6136 on the testing data.

The division algorithm was applied to the sets of symmetrical and antisymmetrical numbers to investigate quotient sets.  It was discovered that dividing symmetrical numbers by positive integers yields antisymmetrical numbers, while dividing antisymmetrical numbers by positive integers results in symmetrical numbers.  Both sets produce the set of integers when divided by integers, resulting in a one-to-one correspondence.  Furthermore, dividing zero by any integer was found to produce zero, and dividing negative integers by other integers was discovered to result in symmetrical numbers.  Finally, Peano induction was used to confirm that these quotient results match the defined structures of symmetrical and antisymmetrical numbers.

Computed Tomography (CT) scans are commonly used in both medical and industrial applications to produce high-quality images of internal structures within objects. Real-world scanners, however, often produce distorted data due to various factors like multiple energy X-ray sources or imperfect detectors. To improve this data, researchers have developed new reconstruction methods that can accurately restore scanned objects while decomposing them into their constituent materials. Our study introduces a unique mathematical framework for processing polyenergetic CT data, which not only enhances the reconstructed image but also identifies the materials present in the scanned object. We demonstrate that this approach leads to a non-convex optimization problem and propose an iterative solution that combines alternating minimization (ALM) techniques. Our results show that this method produces high-quality material decompositions and noise-reduced images, outperforming previous reconstruction methods in terms of accuracy and visual clarity.

Handwritten text recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a challenging problem, primarily due to the scarcity of annotated data and a lack of comprehensive character sets. To overcome this issue, we have developed an innovative approach that simultaneously identifies characters and separates them with non-writing symbols like spaces and line breaks. This approach allows a model to learn how to handle multiple characters and symbols during training. We evaluated our method on a small collection of historical letters from the 16th and 18th centuries and compared it to traditional sequence-to-sequence models. Our results show that the entire collection of approximately 1,600 letters can be accurately recognized in a single pass with our method, achieving a character-level accuracy of 97.6%.

A by-product of extensive nuclear structure computations is a vast amount of data,
such as energy levels, matrix elements, and correlation coefficients. This abstract outlines
a straightforward method to streamline such calculations through a hybrid approach that leverages
different computational techniques with different types of nuclei. Specifically, we've demonstrated
the effectiveness of combining ab initio path integral Monte Carlo and many-body perturbation theory
to study heavy nuclei like $^{48}$Ca. By merging these methods, we've computed a key property, namely the
nuclear energy, by integrating contributions from a perturbation series up to a specified order. Furthermore,
we've examined the feasibility of extrapolating infinite summation of matrix elements, which could have significant
applications in future studies.

We carry out a conceptual examination of quantum transitions within the SSH model, incorporating ideas from algebraic topology, homology, and dynamical systems. We identify novel concepts in quantum transitions, including trajectories, currents, and regions within the lattice, all tied to concepts from algebraic topology. We derive topological properties from these concepts, ultimately extracting essential characteristics via homology, known as quantum topological occurrences. These occurrences serve as a permanent record of the transient dynamics in quantum transitions and retain connections to the underlying topological features of the SSH model.

A biholomorphic map $f$ from one domain to another is considered, with $\Omega$ and $\Omega'$ being convex subsets of $\mathbb{C}^n$ and $\mathbb{C}^m$ respectively. It is known that if $f$ has specific properties and is a compact mapping when applied to $(H^p(\Omega), \|\cdot\|_p)$ for a certain $p > 0$, then it also exhibits compactness when mapped onto $(A^q(\Omega'), \|f\|\otimes \|f^{-1}\|_{\infty})$ for another $q > 0$, provided that certain conditions on $f$ and its inverse are satisfied. 

In this research, we investigate a particular instance of this scenario, with $\Omega$ being a polydisc and $\Omega'$ being a convex analytic disk within the Grassmannian, with the goal of establishing a proof of a previously stated conjecture. Additionally, our methods involve demonstrating that a specific biholomorphic map $f$ from $\Omega$ to $\Omega'$ is a compact mapping when applied to $(H^p(\Omega), \|\cdot\|_p)$ for a certain $p > 0$, by utilizing the F. and M. Riesz convexity theorem and the Aron-Bishop theorem.

We have derived the dual supergravity loops for N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory using AdS_5\times S^5 in the supergravity loop approach. Our method involves a straightforward derivation of the supergravity action and Lagrangian formalism, allowing for a precise comparison with the direct computation of the supergravity loop. Our findings can serve as a test case for the application of the supergravity loop method to more complex theories, such as those beyond N=4 Yang-Mills theory.

This paper introduces DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator designed for GPU use, optimized for object-oriented programming. DynaSOAr is unique in supporting true objects on GPUs, while many existing solutions treat them as structs. By handling memory allocation and deallocation concurrently, DynaSOAr outperforms other allocators, including a comparison method, especially in large-scale applications. DynaSOAr's efficiency is demonstrated across various memory access patterns, including sequential, random, and within-block (within shared memory) access patterns.

We introduce two standard $U(1)_{X}$ models derived from SO(10) by incorporating extra vector-like matter under SO(10). The first model includes one $U(1)_{M}$ alongside a minimal set of three family-dependent $U(1)_{F}$ charges, while the second model features one $U(1)_{M}$ and two universal or nearly universal $U(1)_{{\cal P}_1}$ and $U(1)_{{\cal P}_2}$ charges. By assigning appropriate charge assignments, we investigate the options for obtaining light neutrino masses via the seesaw mechanism, identify suitable proton decay modes, and examine the model's constraints in relation to flavor constraints, anomaly mediation, and the $\mu$ problem. Furthermore, we discuss the potential for electroweak symmetry breaking in these models.

This study investigates the effects of longitudinal stress on metal straw conduits used in high-speed fluid power systems, focusing on their mechanical integrity. A novel, low-cost measurement technique has been developed to quantify both longitudinal stress and the modulus of elasticity for these straws, which are crucial factors in ensuring they can withstand the system's operating pressure. This approach also considers the minimum cross-sectional area of the straw, which is essential for system performance and precision control, especially during startup and shutdown procedures. Our measurements revealed that increasing the modulus of elasticity leads to a slight decrease in longitudinal stress, while elevated temperatures resulted in reduced mechanical integrity of the straw, particularly at the connection points where the seal meets the metal. Furthermore, the study found that the lifespan of the straw could be prolonged by limiting the maximum safe operating pressure, which is calculated based on the modulus of elasticity and specific material properties.

We are given a scenario where we have real-valued functions of unknown variables, and we want to provide guarantees based on their variability for any possible set of functions that could be affected by these variables. This is a Bayesian approach that incorporates our confidence in these variable ranges into our analysis. We can represent the possible distributions of these variables using probabilistic structural identification methods that narrow down possible parameter ranges based on limited measurements. Our approach represents the possible distributions as a combination of probabilistic circuits, and we use constraint propagation to relax the constraints and calculate the coverage of our guarantees for any possible function, representing its confidence interval. This confidence interval can be calculated within a polynomial time of the number of constraints. This framework is useful for guaranteeing the performance of controllers in uncertain systems throughout their entire functional range without necessarily achieving their optimal performance.

In a category-1 (spin-1) superfluid, our proposed setup features a spinning BEC oscillating in a state of multiple quasiparticle creation near an applied magnetic field gradient. This phenomenon bears a striking resemblance to the classic observation of Landau's zitterbewegung. We've developed a simplified theoretical model, confirmed the existence of this oscillation both classically and quantumically, and identified distinct quasi-particle states involved in the process. Furthermore, our findings suggest that quasi-particle creation could lead to the emergence of a robust and detectable signal within an applicable spin-polarized component, potentially allowing for observable signatures via localized measurements.

In generalised quadrangles with automorphism groups that display a neighbor-transitive characteristic, a specific class of linear codes can be formed, which exhibit unique dispersion properties across the quadrangle's geometry. Furthermore, an in-depth analysis has revealed code instances that fail to achieve the maximum possible dispersion, thereby contributing to the existing code literature and deepening our understanding of quadrangles' group properties.

The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) is a highly dense and anisotropically shaped region at the heart of the Milky Way galaxy. To investigate its mass distribution, we analyzed the characteristics of a vast molecular cloud within a 1.5 parsec x 1.5 parsec area. We employed a novel two-dimensional correlation function method on archival VLA radio data. This approach allowed us to quantify the mass distribution of the cloud and determine the anisotropic parameters of its configuration. The results revealed a distinct elliptical shape to the cloud, with its major axis oriented approximately 45 degrees relative to the galactic plane. The anisotropy of the mass distribution became more pronounced as the cloud's density increased. We found that its major and minor axes were proportional to each other, with a constant ratio of about 1.25. We also found that this anisotropic pattern is likely a result of the cloud's dynamics, with its shape influenced by gas streaming from a nearby dense filament. Further analysis is needed to understand the cloud's continued growth and its eventual collapse into new star clusters.

To understand how electrons behave in a high-fluence X-ray absorption edge experiment, a rate model of electron populations is developed within a metal atomic framework. This rate model considers core and valence electron interactions through photon absorption and valence-core electron transitions. Its results reveal that core electron vacancies are replenished at a specific rate after X-ray absorption, leading to distinct S1 and S$\infty$ spectra. Valence electron excitations are also regulated by an equilibrium process, resulting in characteristic broadening of the spectra. This atomic framework approach provides a unified understanding of the spectral shapes near the edge resonance for both linear and high-fluence X-ray absorption spectroscopy.

A minimal yet accurate integrated temperature sensor, suitable for IoT applications with minimal power consumption, is presented. The design utilizes a binary-weighted network consisting of PMOS transistors to measure the voltage across a single thermistor. With a single reference voltage, the proposed design can track temperature changes over a broad range from 0{\deg}C to 150{\deg}C. With a 0.6V to 1.8V supply voltage, the design's energy efficiency is 1.06nJ per conversion and features a 0.24{\deg}C resolution with an error margin of 1.4{\deg}C. The design's functionality and performance were verified using a 0.18$\mu$m CMOS process.

Heralded entanglement creation methods are highly sought after for both experimental and application purposes due to their ability to produce entangled photons with high accuracy. A new technique utilizing quantum scissors has been developed to produce polarization entanglement. This method involves using the scissors operator to cut through a state containing multiple photons, resulting in a variety of outcomes that can each trigger the creation of entangled photons with a specific polarization. By combining this method with practical optical components, a setup has been designed that can create entangled photons with a probability of over 90%, making it suitable for a range of applications including quantum information processing and experiments with quantum gravity.

In virtual problem instances for Euclidean metrics, a (t, k)-approximation algorithm can solve an instance of a specific problem within a factor of t, given that the problem instance is scaled by a factor of k. Achieving perfect T-approximation algorithms for certain problems in scaled instances is equivalent to finding a T-strictly-exhaustive additively-competitive k-weakly-linear cost function for the original instance. Studying such functions is analogous to investigating virtual taxicab spanners. This research focuses on developing the first virtual Euclidean spanners, starting with a (1+1)/2-approximation algorithm for the minimum spanning tree problem, then improving it to obtain a (1+o(1))-approximation algorithm under certain conditions. Further work involves creating the first (1+o)(1)-strictly-exhaustive additively-competitive k-weakly-linear cost function for the Euclidean metric.

In the realm of IoT, managing power consumption is a vital priority due to physical and technical constraints. Since IoT devices often rely on battery power, minimizing their energy usage is essential. Besides optimizing power, there is a growing need for efficient data extraction methods among IoT devices. This is crucial for extracting key features from incoming data without overwhelming the device with processing demands. This research introduces a new method for extracting vital features from wild images using a lightweight encoder, specifically designed to run efficiently on resource-constrained IoT devices. To achieve this, we developed a novel, multi-stage feature extractor that leverages a combination of efficient convolutional and fully connected layers. Additionally, we compared various lightweight encoders and proposed a method for optimizing them to better suit the needs of IoT devices. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed extractor surpasses alternative solutions in both accuracy and computational efficiency.

Godel modal logic encompasses a category of nonclassical logics that are formulated using multimodal systems with an emphasis on normal modal logic principles. To capture the behavior of the modal operators, we introduce two distinct algebraic structures: a canonical modal algebra based on the concept of nerves, and a more fundamental modal algebra built upon the principles of multivalued lattice-ordered groups. Additionally, we propose an extension to traditional Kripke models that incorporates the ability to represent "knowing that one knows" in a systematic manner. This methodology leads to the development of corresponding modal languages, which in turn allow us to demonstrate a duality between the categories of Godel modal algebras and Godel modal Kripke frames. Furthermore, we present a unified approach to the representation theory of Godel modal algebras, which offers a versatile framework for mathematical and computational applications.

This research presents a novel technique for word-alignment that leverages data from either monolingual or bilingual external sources. Our method generates word alignments in a sentence-by-sentence basis without requiring pre-training. It can be applied in settings where comprehensive training is unfeasible due to limited data availability. Instead, the system utilizes available bilingual data to determine a suitable mapping between sentences, which is then utilized for sentence-by-sentence word alignment. Additionally, our method enables the incorporation of semantic information by treating sentences as unitary semantic entities. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our method achieves comparable results on IWSLT en-de datasets when supplemented with SEMEKk data, a bilingual resource. Alternatively, on IWSLT fr-en datasets, our method performs better than the standard GIZA++ when supplemented with Prodigy monolingual annotations.

The distorted resolvent method offers a straightforward approach to construct Nash equilibria for various classes of Nash games, including monotone, uniformly Lipschitz, and Lipschitz games. This method provides precise estimates of the distance between the distorted resolvent of the best response function and the identity operator, which in turn yields precise estimates of the error in approximating Nash equilibria via the fixed point iteration method. This results in a constructive proof of the finite number of steps required to achieve a Nash equilibrium via this method in finite games. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the method facilitates convergence analysis of various iterative algorithms for finite games, and offers an alternative means of deriving existence results for Nash equilibria via the fixed point theorem.

If primordial black holes exist in sufficient quantities, they could act as a significant form of dark energy responsible for accelerating the universe's expansion. Due to their elusive nature, it's difficult to verify PBHs' existence, but their potential impact on the universe's evolution makes it worthwhile. To explore PBHs' effect on the cosmos, researchers use computational models. In this study, we examine a dark energy model involving PBHs, implemented using the PopSyCLE code, a parallel computational tool designed to model PBHs' effect on the universe. Through a series of simulations, we investigate how various model parameters, including PBH mass and density, affect cosmological observations. These findings serve as a foundation for future research using the PopSyCLE code, including the analysis of N-body simulations and the development of new algorithms.

A comprehensive study on the configuration of balls in a two-dimensional space was conducted, with the primary goal of identifying the diversity of arrangements and their stability when subjected to a continuous rotation modulated by a sine wave. Through both computer simulations and theoretical analysis, it was found that the majority of configurations could be categorized into either a compact form with all balls at the perimeter or an extended shape with balls positioned at local minima of the potential energy function. Furthermore, by applying the concept of Lyapunov spaces, it was discovered that the stability of these configurations could be quantitatively evaluated. Notably, it was observed that an infinite number of stable configurations exist in addition to three well-documented states of perpetual rotation, with each of these stable configurations exhibiting uniqueness and invariance to changes in the system's parameters.

The classical Poisson equation was devised for a constant source term and solved for a constant potential in an incompressible fluid flow scenario. In the context of spherical harmonics and Green's functions, this equation can be utilized to model random field phenomena on a sphere by assuming a field is the sum of a constant field and a randomly varying field. By applying a forward filtering approach, this scenario can be represented as a linear state-space model, which is characterized by one-step forward-recurrent dynamics. As an alternative to traditional spatial statistical models, this recursive framework offers a unified approach to field estimation, prediction, interpolation, and extrapolation.

Single-pixel visualization technology has significant potential for applications in optics, particularly for viewing complex two-dimensional light patterns with high resolution. However, the advancement of this field is constrained by the availability of undetected single photons. We overcame this limitation by developing an innovative quantum protocol that relies on undetected single photons and does not require participants. This new approach leads to the implementation of a reliable single-pixel image rendering method. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our solution, we successfully created and tested a quantum black and white image viewer.

Despite the long history of foam research, the origin of friction when two foams come into contact has not been fully explained. Our study reveals that friction in foams is primarily caused by the interaction of surfaces with irregularities, which lead to the creation of stable bubbles at the point of contact. Our experiments demonstrate that the frictional force exerted by one foam on another varies systematically with the size of the bubbles in both substances and is not significantly affected by differences in liquid solution properties. This observation suggests that friction in foams is governed by a universal mechanism involving the creation of bubble structures, which can occur in any liquid solution.

This study focuses on identifying skin carcinomas through image analysis, a crucial technique for diagnosing the condition. Due to the diverse nature of carcinomas (both superficial and deep), distinguishing them from benign lesions and healthy skin requires consideration of multiple features. However, tumors appearing at varying depths have distinct visual appearances, making it necessary to weigh their importance differently. By combining decision-making from multiple models and utilizing the information of two entropy-based spatial information measures, we can effectively identify outliers among training data, thereby improving classification performance. Our proposed method achieves top outcomes in the 2017, 2018, and 2020 ISIC challenge.

We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium, employing both monochromatic and pulse-powered X-ray radiation. By doing so, we observed the decay process of electron holes created by core-level excitations and analyzed the resulting electron-hole recombination dynamics. Our experimental results indicated that sodium meets the criteria for an almost-free electron metal with an extremely long electron lifetime, in agreement with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we verified that recombination occurs through a homogeneous process and discovered that sodium's electron lifetime is significantly longer than calculated by Elliott's theory, primarily due to an underestimation of sodium's effective mass in the metal state.

To analyze molecular dynamics, initial conditions are assigned to N identical copies of the system, and their phase space evolution is monitored as their Hamiltonian changes. However, the variation in their initial states poses a challenge, causing some to undergo unwanted transformations. A new technique has been developed to address this issue, allowing the assignment of initial conditions that minimize these changes while maintaining optimal performance. This method is particularly useful for studying the free expansion of microspheres and has been successfully applied in such simulations.

The study of graph-based formalism provides a valuable approach to understanding local coordinates of symplectic structure expansion. A key concept in this framework is the 'weight' of a graph, which is calculated through a process called sum-over-tau. In our research, we have developed a method to calculate the weights of link and curvature graphs in relation to a fixed connection, using a symplectic structure as a reference point. This calculation is based on a specific infinite series, which is defined by the structure's expansion.

We have investigated the dynamics of a feebly nonlinear woodpile and diatomic granular chain. By applying the continuum approximation and considering only the largest terms in the expansion, we have derived a simplified model. This model reveals the presence of solitary waves, similar to those found in the N- and T-polarized modes of a strongly nonlinear woodpile chain. The amplitude of these solitary waves is determined by the parameters of the system, specifically the granular chain's length and stiffness, as well as the size of the excitation.

Our research expands on cosmological collider physics, exploring a novel scenario in which the signal's amplitude isn't significantly impacted by primordial features. Instead, we investigate how the symmetry breaking of spontaneous symmetry breaking influences the momentum regime of the signal, which is characterized by a sharp peak at twice the particle's mass. Additionally, we identify two distinct momentum regimes in which the signal is produced, separated by the Hubble rate. One regime is produced by particles with similar momenta, while the other regime is essentially a delta function, primarily influenced by particles with negligible momenta.

A graph and its "accordion" transformation are introduced, which adds new vertices and edges to a given graph by shifting and expanding its existing cycles. This paper explores the properties of accordion graphs obtained from quartic circulant graphs by applying this transformation.
